title: Eliminate unresolved broadcasts
author: jacobhinkle
body: While implementing concretization of dynamic resizes (#258), it occurred to me that we should handle this particular type of concretization more generally. The only reason resize is a dynamic operation is that the output might have an extent equal to 1. We currently mark IterDomains with extent 1 as Broadcast so that they maintain the ability to broadcast when they're used in later expressions. However, we don't actually check that they ever are used this way. That means that if users pass inputs that sometimes have size one in some dimension (such as a batch or channel dimension) they will not be able to re-use kernels for size >1 even when that should be possible. In the short term, this also means that we cannot use cat along size-1 dimensions (#224). One reason not to eliminate broadcasts too hastily is that one might add new expressions to the Fusion right up until the point that it's lowered. Even if we don't expect that to happen, until the concretization phase was introduced in #24 it was not clear at which point we even should attempt to clear out unresolved broadcasts. Now that we have a concretization stage and will soon have an "initial info" building stage of concretization (#244), there is a natural place to put this analysis. Propagation of broadcast removal When an IterDomain, bS0, with IterType equal to Broadcast is used in an operation in a position that aligns with another IterDomain, iS1, of type Iteration, we say that this "resolves" the broadcast bS0. This is an important event since it means we cannot use identical indexing for iS1 and bS0, and we instead need to collapse the iS1 index to 0 when using it in place of bS0. Note that bS0 (or its TensorView) may appear in multiple Exprs, so there may be zero or multiple resolutions of a given broadcast. If there are zero resolutions of bS0, this means that any Exprs it appeared in contained other expressions that aligned perfectly; i.e. there either were no other expressions, they were unary, or other arguments also had broadcast IterDomains in the aligned position. In this case, the behavior is no different from if the IterType of bS0 had been Iteration to begin with. Aside: connecting the ID subgraph To better facilitate analyzing broadcasts, it might be useful to explicitly connect the IterDomain subgraph of the Fusion. Note that of course the Fusion contains enough information to do the analysis as-is, but it is not very ergonomic. To see this, consider a simple unary op like neg. Consider the following Fusion:   auto tv0 = makeConcreteTensor({3, 5});   fusion->addInput(tv0);   auto tv1 = makeConcreteTensor({3, 5});   fusion->addInput(tv1);   auto tv2 = mul(tv0, tv1);   fusion->addOutput(tv2);   fusion->printMath(); // Inputs: //   T0_g[ iS0{3}, iS1{5} ], float //   T1_g[ iS2{3}, iS3{5} ], float // Outputs: //   T2_g[ iS4{3}, iS5{5} ], float   // The following all print 0   std::cout << tv0->getMaybeRFactorDomain()[0]->uses().size() << std::endl;   std::cout << tv0->getMaybeRFactorDomain()[1]->uses().size() << std::endl;   std::cout << tv1->getMaybeRFactorDomain()[0]->uses().size() << std::endl;   std::cout << tv1->getMaybeRFactorDomain()[1]->uses().size() << std::endl;   std::cout << (void*)tv2->getRootDomain()[0]->definition() << std::endl;   std::cout << (void*)tv2->getRootDomain()[1]->definition() << std::endl; None of the IterDomains are tracking uses or definitions, even though iS4 and iS5 are clearly derived from [iS0, iS2] and [iS1, iS3] respectively. I suggest we make this clear so that we can more easily inspect the actual dependencies between IterDomain.s To do this, we can introduce a new op type, tentatively called Align and a corresponding align(std::vector<IterDomain*> ids, Expr* expr) op. The Align op would hold the ids in its inputs() and it would hold a reference to the expression it appeared in as an attribute. We would modify ops::newOutputTV to use the align op to create new IterDomains and assemble them into a TensorDomain, instead of using IterDomainBuilder directly as is done currently through newOutputDomain. With that change, the Fusion above would have two new Align expressions producing the IDs iS4 and iS5, so that we could traverse from outputs to inputs without having to wind through the TV machinery (other than acquiring the output IDs in the first step). Changing the Fusion by adding new Exprs runs the risk of winding up in an inconsistent state, so care must be taken when replacing IterDomains that their history be preserved properly. Detecting unresolved Broadcast at concretization After our current concretization is run (resolves all Symbolic IDs to Broadcast or Iteration), we would pass through all Align expressions to find broadcast resolutions. There is room for improvement here, but a naive algorithm would just mark each Broadcast input that is aligned with at least one concrete ID as "resolved". Then if an ID does not have any resolved uses(), it is safe to set it to type Iteration. This would automatically mark all output non-reduction IDs as Iteration. Detecting unresolved Broadcast before concretization After we are comfortable eliminating broadcasts at concretization, we can push further to eliminate both broadcasts as well as symbolic IDs before we receive inputs. We can do this in much the same way as we do at concretization, but we need to be careful when handling Symbolic inputs. However, for example, if we have Symbolic IDs that only appear in unary ops before appearing in an output, these can safely be set to Iteration. Similarly, we can often reason about the equality of extents before we have concrete inputs (moreso once we address #320), and if we can prove equality of extents then we can prove an Align of Symbolic IDs is non-resolving, etc. Plan I suggest that once #244 is merged, we add a stage that attempts to remove unresolved Broadcasts from the (still possibly dynamic) Fusion. Removing broadcasts would propagate upstream, since if there are no downstream broadcasts, we may also be able to change upstream Symbolic IDs to Iteration. Note that Symbolic is also used for reshape, but this should not interfere with concretization of reshapes since we already store the locations of dynamic reshapes when building concretization information, and we replace them during concretization; we should just be sure that IDs are connected properly by static reshape so that the graph is reconnected during concretization. ### Tasks - [ ] Connect the IterDomain subgraph by introducing Align op - [ ] Remove unresolved Broadcasts during concretization - [ ] Remove unresolved symbolic branches before concretization

title: IterDomain cannot be both a broadcast and rfactor domain
author: jacobhinkle
body: The pad op expands root IterDomains by calling resize and marking them as rfactor IDs. The IterType of the resized IterDomain will be Broadcast if the extent is 1, which happens for example if the pad widths are negative and sum to one less than the input extent. In such cases, we hit an assertion in the IterDomain constructor that an rfactor domain cannot be marked Broadcast. There is currently a commented case that triggers this error in the DynamicPadShmoo_CUDA test in #258, but a minimal example is: // Test setting an rfactor domain that is of IterType Broadcast TEST_F(NVFuserTest, FusionBroadcastRFactorID_CUDA) {   Fusion fusion;   // Try to create an extent-1 Broadcast IterDomain that is marked rfactor   IterDomainBuilder(fusion.zeroVal(), fusion.oneVal())           .is_rfactor_domain(true)           .iter_type(IterType::Broadcast)           .build();   // The above throws the following exception in .build():   // IterDomain cannot be both a broadcast and rfactor domain.   // Exception raised from IterDomain at /opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/ir_nodes.cpp:2105 }

title: Symbolic iter domains should not exact map when aligned
author: jacobhinkle
body: I am trying to make the following test pass: // Test dynamic pad followed by broadcast resolution TEST_F(NVFuserTest, DynamicPadBroadcast_CUDA) {   std::unique_ptr<Fusion> fusion_ptr = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   Fusion& fusion = *fusion_ptr.get();   FusionGuard fg(&fusion);    TensorView* tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(2);   fusion.addInput(tv0);   TensorView* tv1 = makeSymbolicTensor(2);   fusion.addInput(tv1);    // 2d axis order here is YX   auto ypad = IrBuilder::create<Int>();   fusion.addInput(ypad);   auto xpad = IrBuilder::create<Int>();   fusion.addInput(xpad);    // two-way resizes to cut square tv down to broadcastable size in either axis   auto tv0_pad = pad(tv0, {fusion.zeroVal(), xpad, fusion.zeroVal(), ypad});    // This will potentially resolve the y or x broadcast   auto p = mul(tv0_pad, tv1);   fusion.addOutput(p);    fusion.printMath(); /* Inputs:                                                                                                                             T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ], float                                                                                                   T1_g[ iS2{i3}, iS3{i4} ], float                                                                                                   i5, int64_t                                                                                                                       i6, int64_t                                                                                                                     Outputs:                                                                                                                            T3_g[ iS8{( i0 + i5 )}, iS9{( i2 + i6 )} ], float                                                                                                                                                                                                                 %kernel_math {                                                                                                                    T2_l[ ?S5{( i0 + i5 )}rf, ?S7{( i2 + i6 )}rf ]                                                                                       = pad( T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ], {0, i5, 0, i6} )                                                                              T3_g[ iS8{( i0 + i5 )}, iS9{( i2 + i6 )} ]                                                                                           = T2_l[ ?S5{( i0 + i5 )}rf, ?S7{( i2 + i6 )}rf ]                                                                                  * T1_g[ iS2{i3}, iS3{i4} ];                                                                                                    } */    FusionExecutorCache fusion_executor_cache(std::move(fusion_ptr));    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   at::Tensor at_x = at::randn({5, 5}, options);   at::Tensor at_y = at::randn({5, 5}, options);    std::vector<c10::IValue> aten_inputs({at_x, at_y, 0, 0});   std::vector<at::Tensor> outputs;    // shrink first axis so that the multiplication resolves a broadcast   aten_inputs[2] = -4;   aten_inputs[3] = 0;   outputs = fusion_executor_cache.runFusionWithInputs(aten_inputs);   testValidate(fusion_executor_cache.fusion(), outputs, aten_inputs, {at_x[0].unsqueeze(0) * at_y}, __LINE__, __FILE__); } During concretization, we try and evaluate the extent of dynamic resize. In this case, we want to evaluate extents of ?S5{( i0 + i5 )}rf and ?S7{( i2 + i6 )}rf. To compute these we use an expression evaluator, which actually throws an error:  C++ exception with description "known_size == this_size INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/expr_evaluator.cpp":210, please report a bug to PyTorch. Conflicting sizes: 5, 1  The following initial values are bound correctly based on inputs:  Binding 5 to i0 Binding 5 to i2 Binding 5 to i3 Binding 5 to i4 Binding -4 to i5 Binding 0 to i6  The error comes in ExpressionEvaluator::propagateBoundValuesThroughExactMaps when evaluating i0 + i5 which evaluates to 1 but has known_size == 5. I believe this is because earlier, the multiplication sees a Symbolic domain aligned with an Iteration domain and interprets this as an exact map. I think the fix is to adjust the exact map condition to never set an exact mapping to/from Symbolic domains.

author: jacobhinkle

The size-1 slice   // could be size >1 with no change in the error. The order does not   // matter. Performing only one of these slices does not trigger the   // error and the output is correct in that case. If there are   // multiple size-0 slices the error is not triggered. It only seems   // to appear when there are both size-0 and size non-zero slices of   // the same tensor.   auto tv1 = slice(       tv0,       {{IrBuilder::create<Int>(0),         IrBuilder::create<Int>(1),         IrBuilder::create<Int>(1)}});   fusion->addOutput(tv1);   auto tv2 = slice(       tv0,       {{IrBuilder::create<Int>(0),         IrBuilder::create<Int>(0),         IrBuilder::create<Int>(1)}});   fusion->addOutput(tv2);    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   at::manual_seed(0);    auto t0 = at::randn(shape, options);   std::vector<c10::IValue> aten_inputs({t0});    FusionExecutorCache executor_cache(std::move(fusion));   auto cg_outputs = executor_cache.runFusionWithInputs(aten_inputs);    auto ref0 = t0.index({at::indexing::Slice(0, 1)});   auto ref1 = t0.index({at::indexing::Slice(0, 0)});    TORCH_CHECK(ref0.equal(cg_outputs[0]));   TORCH_CHECK(ref1.equal(cg_outputs[1])); } This gives an error during scheduling:  C++ exception with description "!new_numerator_val->isZeroInt() && (!new_numerator_val->isConstInt() || new_numerator_val->evaluateInt() > 0) INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/scheduler/vectorize_helper.h":74, please report a bug to PyTorch. Adding numerator value of zero not supported in ProjectedExtent.  This is coming from getPointwiseHeuristics calling getAllVectorizedMapsOf->ContiguousInnerDimensionsMapper::map. My naive thought is to just extent ProjectedExtent to handle size-0 dimensions, but I want to be sure that doesn't violate any assumptions in uses of that class first.

Exception raised from split at /opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/ir_nodes.cpp:2333  This happens when we choose a reference tensor that's not empty, but attempt to replay transforms on a size-0 tensor. We probably just need to carefully add size-0 support in IterDomain::split. Note that other incantations also expose this limitation in Merge so they should both be tested.

title: Squeeze fails on Symbolic input
author: jacobhinkle
body: With dynamic fusions we may not be able to prove that an axis is size-1 before it is used in a squeeze operation. Currently, squeeze has a static shape API, but even then it requires the squeezed dimensions to be broadcast, and that check fails with Symbolic inputs even if they later are concretized to Broadcast. // Test squeezing a symbolic dimension TEST_F(NVFuserTest, FusionSqueezeSymbolic_CUDA) {   auto fusion = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   FusionGuard fg(fusion.get());    std::vector<int64_t> shape({4, 5});    // concrete shapes to avoid dynamic Fusion   auto tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(2);   fusion->addInput(tv0);    auto s1 = IrBuilder::create<Int>();   fusion->addInput(s1);   auto numel_symb = mul(tv0->axis(0)->extent(), tv0->axis(1)->extent());   auto tv1 = reshape(tv0, {s1, ceilDiv(numel_symb, s1)});   // tv1 should have symbolic output IterTypes, so squeeze should accept   // symbolic, and concretization should fail if symbolic squeeze input is not   // concretized to Broadcast   // NOTE: squeeze interface should be updated to match reshape and friends, accepting Val inputs   auto tv2 = squeeze(tv1, {20, 1}, 1);   // tv1 is of shape {0, 5}   fusion->addOutput(tv2);    FusionExecutorCache fec(std::move(fusion));    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   at::manual_seed(0);    auto t0 = at::randn(shape, options);   std::vector<c10::IValue> aten_inputs({t0, 20});    auto cg_outputs = fec.runFusionWithInputs(aten_inputs);    auto ref0 = t0.flatten();    TORCH_CHECK(ref0.equal(cg_outputs[0])); }  C++ exception with description "Can not squeeze non-broadcasting dimension(s). Exception raised from squeeze at /opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/ops/alias.cpp:194  The immediate fix is to accept either Symbolic or Broadcast inputs at definition, then check that there are no non-Broadcast inputs to SqueezeOp after concretization.

title: Support squeeze with dynamic shapes in Python frontend
author: jacobhinkle
body: fd.ops.squeeze currently requires a static input shape to be provided as a list of ints, along with a list of dims to squeeze, matching the C++ call to squeeze in SqueezeOpRecord. We should instead convert both to match the alternative interface: TORCH_CUDA_CU_API TensorView* squeeze(     TensorView* x,     const std::vector<bool>& to_squeeze); This will enable symbolic shapes to be more easily handled; see #379.

title: Resolve Symbolic inputs to SqueezeOp and ExpandOp
author: jacobhinkle
body: Consider the following Fusion: auto tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(1);  // [ iS0{i0} ] auto s1 = IrBuilder::create<Int>(); auto s2 = IrBuilder::create<Int>(); fusion.addInput(tv0); fusion.addInput(s1); fusion.addInput(s2);  auto tv3 = reshape(tv0, {s1, s2}); // Dynamic reshape output: [ ?S1{s1}, ?S2{s2} ] auto tv4 = add(tv3, tv3);  // [ ?S3{s1}, ?S4{s2} ] // Squeeze should resolve ?S4 and ?S2 to Broadcast auto tv5 = squeeze(tv4, {1}); // [ ?S5{s1} ] fusion.addOutput(tv5); Since the input IDs to any squeeze or expand call must be Broadcast, the presence of such a call implies that the input doesn't need to be Symbolic and can be marked Broadcast ahead of concretization (like within the squeeze and expand ops). It also implies a constraint that the extent (i.e. s2) should be 1, which is something that needs to be checked at runtime so that we know this structural implication is valid. Concretization of these broadcasts is similar to the runtime issue of eliminating unresolved broadcasts (see #340), but is triggered during Fusion definition. We should resolve these types of structural implications ahead of time whenever possible. Pitfalls Imagine we have another use for tv3: // ... auto tv6 = mul (tv3, tv3);  // [ ?S6{s1}, ?S7{s2} ] fusion.addOutput(tv6); This branch can also benefit from the proposed "definition-time concretization" by replacing ?S7{s2} with bS8{s2}. Thus we need to traverse in both directions to ensure the entire exact mapping group is properly concretized. Approach I think that early in the squeeze and expand ops we should detect symbolic IterDomains that must be Broadcast, and kick off a new traversal that starts at a given set of IterDomains in a given TensorView, then sets the IterType to Broadcast in their entire exact mapped group. If the input is Symbolic its extent will depend on input shapes or input scalars (like s2 above), so we should be careful to check somewhere that the inputs are consistent with the extent == 1 constraint. This could be done via a general mechanism where we attach Bool scalars to the Fusion object which will be checked against inputs. Alternatively, we could update the checkConcretization machinery from #380  to validate inputs not just at concretization but at runtime.

title: Dynamic reshape with concrete output shape
author: jacobhinkle
body: The reshape op takes an input TensorView and a vector of scalars which describe the output shape. Neither that argument nor the input shape need to be concrete. If either of the input or output shapes are not concrete, the op is described as a "dynamic reshape", since we cannot know how to decompose it into Merge and Split operations until we have concrete input and output shapes. (Note that this may not be strictly true in the future if we add the ability to prove some equalities at the definition stage with dynamic shapes (see #320 and #382)) The way we currently signal that a reshape is dynamic is by creating a placeholder rfactor domain that is disconnected with the root domain and whose IterDomains are all Symbolic. While we do need a way to easily determine that a ViewOp is dynamic, setting the outputs to Symbolic introduces complexity that cascades to downstream ops: every reshape and most resize ops that follow downstream will be dynamic since the inputs will be Symbolic. // A dynamic reshape op with symbolic input shape, but concrete output shape TEST_F(NVFuserTest, DynamicReshapeConcreteOutput_CUDA) {   Fusion fusion;   FusionGuard fg(&fusion);   auto tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(2);   fusion.addInput(tv0);   // Constant output extents should not result in Symbolic IterDomains   auto reshape_shape0 = IrBuilder::create<Int>(3);   auto reshape_shape1 = IrBuilder::create<Int>(5);   auto tv2 = reshape(tv0, {reshape_shape0, reshape_shape1});   auto tv3 = add(tv2, tv2);   fusion.addOutput(tv3);   fusion.print();   /*   %kernel {   T1_l[ ?S4{3}rf, ?S5{5}rf ] = view( T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ] )   T2_g[ ?S6{3}, ?S7{5} ]      = T1_l[ ?S4{3}rf, ?S5{5}rf ]      + T1_l[ ?S4{3}rf, ?S5{5}rf ];    TransformPrinter :   T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ]    root domain : (iS0{i0}, iS1{i2})    contiguity: f f    leaf domain : (iS0{i0}, iS1{i2})   T1_l[ ?S4{3}rf, ?S5{5}rf ]    root domain : (iS2{i0}, iS3{i2})    rfactor domain : (?S4{3}rf, ?S5{5}rf)    contiguity: t t    leaf domain : (?S4{3}rf, ?S5{5}rf)   T2_g[ ?S6{3}, ?S7{5} ]    root domain : (?S6{3}, ?S7{5})    contiguity: t t    leaf domain : (?S6{3}, ?S7{5})    */ } Instead of using the output rfactor domain itertypes to signal that an op is dynamic, we should do something like the following:  Update the reshape op to set the output rfactor IterTypes to non-Symbolic values whenever possible. Set the output's root IterDomains to Symbolic whenever an input is neither Broadcast or has constant extent. The reason to allow non-symbolic Broadcast in the root is that the Broadcast itertype's presence attests that the extent is 1. Update logic in dynamic_transform.cpp to ensure that we still detect that these reshapes are dynamic.

title: Persistent buffer selection: cache var used by each iteration in grid persistent kernel, e.g. weight in layer norm backward #2525
author: liqiangxl
body: Moved from csarofeen/pytorch#2525 In layer norm backward: For input DataType::Half, the persistent buffers are projected to three inputs (dy, x, weight), total size is 3 * sizeof(half) * dim1 For input DataType::Float the persistent buffers are NOT projected, they are xhat and d_xhat, the total size is 2 * sizeof(float) * dim1 If I enforce projection for input DataType::Float, there is a significiant speedup, e.g. for case 2048 x 10240 the time is reduced from 274 us to 207 us, for case 2048 x 1024 the time is reduced from 39 us to 36 us. The reason is because weight is shared across different rows. If we keep it persistent, we don't need to reload it in the iteration over different rows. The projected version needs more registers per thread but it doesn't reduce the occupancy ratio as the all the blocks must be active at the same time for this grid persistent kernel.

title: Error in getCompiledKernel when no at::Tensors have been initialized
author: jacobhinkle
body: It seems likely that our method of initializing and handling cuda contexts has a bug that the new device option for fd.execute is exposing. We are currently seeing CI failures using CUDA 11.7 and 11.8, but not 12.1 (see https://gitlab-master.nvidia.com/dl/pytorch/fuser-gh-mirror/-/jobs/61379693). The error is context was destroyed during the test_selected_device python frontend test. This occurs when trying to load the compiled cuda kernel as a CUmodule at https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/csrc/executor_utils.cpp#L1122. We currently call at::cuda::jit::initializeCudaContext() at https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/csrc/executor_utils.cpp#L1377. This is after using c10::DeviceGuard to properly set the device to 1 in this case. It seems there is some issue with how we are initializing the default context though, since it is not properly set later (line 1122). PyTorch initializes the context correctly, so in most cases, it will have already done so since we will have input tensors residing on the selected device before compiling the Fusion. That must be the case, for example, if any of the inputs to the Fusion are tensors. However, in the test at hand, there are no input tensors. Since PyTorch initializes the context, a very simple work-around for the test is to swap these lines: https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/python_tests/test_python_frontend.py#L2133-L2134. After swapping, the definition of eager_out will initialize the CUDA context on device 1, and the test will pass.

title: Slice should clip to end of tensor
author: jacobhinkle
body: Slice behavior currently does not match numpy/PyTorch when the end_indices extend past the tensor extent: // Slice with end beyond size of input. This should clip to input, not pad. TEST_F(NVFuserTest, FusionResizeSlice6_CUDA) {   Fusion fusion;   FusionGuard fg(&fusion);    std::vector<int64_t> shape({9});    // concrete shapes to avoid dynamic Fusion   auto tv0 = makeConcreteTensor(shape);   fusion.addInput(tv0);    auto tv1 = slice(tv0, {{fusion.zeroVal(), IrBuilder::create<Int>(11)}});   fusion.addOutput(tv1);    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);    auto t0 = at::randn(shape, options);   std::vector<c10::IValue> aten_inputs({t0});    FusionExecutor fe;   fe.compileFusion(&fusion, aten_inputs);   auto cg_outputs = fe.runFusion(aten_inputs);    auto ref = t0.index({at::indexing::Slice(0, 11)});    testValidate(&fusion, cg_outputs, aten_inputs, {ref}, __LINE__, __FILE__);   // C++ exception with description "The size of tensor a (9) must match the   // size of tensor b (11) at non-singleton dimension 0 Exception raised from   // infer_size_impl at /opt/pytorch/pytorch/aten/src/ATen/ExpandUtils.cpp:31 } In these cases, we should clip to the end of the tensor. That is, we should implicitly use min(extent, end_index) instead of index itself. As discussed in #397 this means we should not concretize slice ops prematurely unless we know their input extents.

title: nonlinear increase of registers if there are two persistent buffers
author: liqiangxl
body: During the work of #401, we noticed the nonlinear increase of registers if there are two persistent buffers also the persistent batch of 8 is slower than batch of 4. These two interesting results are against our general assumptions: (1) Prefer smaller thread blocks with larger work-per-thread factors. Compared to larger blocks with smaller work per thread, it should lead to more efficient register usage, which would make the overall effective occupancy higher and achieve better performance (2) Register usage count should linearly depend on the per-thread work factor Needs to investigate why.

title: Efficient metadata-only segments
author: jacobhinkle
body: We sometimes segment Fusions into segments containing a single operation that is equivalent to a copy. For example, when we begin a fusion with a reshape operation that splits an axis and then we perform a reduction over only one of those axes: see csarofeen/pytorch#2090 and #418. In these cases the segmentation actually often simplifies the remaining fusion segments and it's only inefficient because we do not skip compiling and launching a CUDA kernel. I will refer to these as NoKernel segments since they don't require launching a kernel. They are distinguished from NoOp segments which do launch a kernel, but which might operate on a single value (i.e. only zero-dimensional tensors). We should process these simple NoKernel segments efficiently without compiling or launching new kernels. Since they will be efficient and potentially can help simplify the remaining segments in a Fusion, the segmenter should try to segment them out as much as possible in cases when there is no downside to doing so. One such scenario is at the beginning of each Fusion segment. Removing NoKernel segments from the beginning of a complete Fusion is of particular interest, but these segments can also appear internal to a segmented Fusion or at the end. I am not sure whether explicitly trying to remove NoKernel segments from the end of the complete Fusion (or from the end of a segment) would be beneficial; if a scheduler heuristic has accepted the segment, might we obtain better performance by removing some trailing metadata ops in some cases? Approach If a complete Fusion cannot be scheduled in a single segment, segmentation is performed by building up segments one expression at a time. That means that we can identify some fusable NoKernel segments by testing if they can be evaluated without a kernel. The first time we identify an expression that requires a kernel, we will then roll back and use the prior expressions (if there were any) in a NoKernel segment. This requires a light modification to the current segmenting code in order to enable this special greedy behavior in the NoKernel scheduler; otherwise the NoKernel expressions might be accepted by other schedulers like NoOp and Pointwise and we will fail to segment these "free" NoKernel expressions at the beginning of the segment. Note that this approach allows us to identify some NoKernel segments that are internal to the Fusion; not just those at the beginning or end of the complete Fusion. I propose we identify ops that can be computed without launching a CUDA kernel. For now I think this is an exhaustive list:  reshape, which we can sometimes replace with at::view. This replacement is not possible if strides/contiguity are incompatible. The condition under which we can do the replacement can be decomposed into a decision for each axis merge/split. We can always split an axis, regardless of its contiguity; the output's inner axis will have the same contiguity of the input and the outer output axis will be contiguous. For a merge of two axes, the outer axis must be contiguous and the resulting merged axis will have the contiguity of the input inner axis. permute & transpose slice, which we can replace with tensor.narrow. Likewise pad with non-positive extents. Factory methods like full, if we are able to prove that at least one of the extents is zero. set which is a complete metadata copy. any scalar expression which we can evaluate with an ExpressionEvaluator.  FusionExecutor can inspect an input Fusion to determine whether or not it is metadata-only. However, whether or not we evaluate it that way may depend on the segment's context in the surrounding complete Fusion.  For the TensorView ops, we need to ensure that we don't break any implicit aliasing assumptions. In particular, unless requested to alias an input of the Fusion, we should ensure that if the output of a metadata-only segment is not marked as aliasing an input, that we perform the copy if needed. This type of alias analysis should not be too hard since we already have io_alias_. It can be done in SegmentedFusion which handles the set of FusionExecutors and can coordinate which of these performs metadata-only ops instead of compiling a new kernel for them. FusionExecutor would then be in charge of evaluating each of the inputs. ### Tasks - [ ] Create greedy `NoKernel` scheduler - [ ] Evaluate metadata ops directly in `FusionExecutor`

However, group 2 can't be launched because the first extent i0 is not available. This is because bS0{i0} has extent 1 but its expandedExtent is i0, and we only make extent() available as an input. In order to properly accept expanded inputs, we should probably at minimum change FusionKernelRuntime::prepareRuntimeOrder to use getMaybeExpandedExtent() instead of extent() when finding available inputs. That happens to fix this particular issue, but more testing should probably done specifically for expanded inputs in segmented Fusions.

title: Feature: allow explicit manipulation of Philox RNG state via functional version of RNG ops
author: IvanYashchuk
body: The request is to implement TensorView functional_uniform(Val* philox_seed, Val* philox_offset, const std::vector<Val*>& shape,  Val* low,  Val* high, DataType dtype) and the corresponding Python bindings. This operation should not increase nvFuser's rand_offset defined here                Fuser/csrc/executor.cpp                   Lines 1460 to 1468       in       730215f                                                 uint64_t rand_offset = 0;                                           if (kernel()->summary().max_rng_offsets >= 0) {                                             // NOTE: this is how we map offset to PW kernels in order to have                                             // identical random number generator to match native PyTorch results.                                             // But it doesn't really work as it takes assumption how threads are                                             // binded but is not generally how we handle that in scheduler.                                             // Refer to `Philox` in generated kernel to understand how the mapping                                             // works.                                             rand_offset = (uint64_t)(kernel()->summary().max_rng_offsets + 1) * 4;                     because it's essentially a deterministic operation. In addition, the result should be independent of the chosen vectorization, but I think it is already implemented by using linear index here                Fuser/csrc/codegen.cpp                    Line 706       in       730215f                                                 indent() << "nvfuser_index_t linear_index" << rop->name() << " = " << index                     Motivation Currently, nvFuser has two random ops uniform and normal. Internally it uses a Philox PRNG and its state is tied to PyTorch's RNG state. For each kernel invocation nvFuser is advancing PyTorch's RNG by the number of random ops in a kernel:                Fuser/csrc/executor_kernel_arg.cpp                   Lines 603 to 614       in       730215f                                                 void KernelArgumentHolder::appendPhiloxRNGSeed(uint64_t rand_offset) {                                             at::PhiloxCudaState philox_engine_inputs;                                             auto gen = at::cuda::detail::getDefaultCUDAGenerator();                                             {                                               // See Note [Acquire lock when using random generators]                                               std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(gen.mutex());                                               philox_engine_inputs =                                                   at::check_generator<at::CUDAGeneratorImpl>(gen)->philox_cuda_state(                                                       rand_offset);                                             }                                             push(philox_engine_inputs);                                           }                     That offers a great eager-like experience and torch.manual_seed and torch.random.fork_rng behaves as expected with nvFuser kernel invocations. However, there are cases where explicit seed manipulation might be more efficient, for example, for dropout backward it's sufficient to save the Philox seed to recompute the dropout mask during backward instead of saving the mask from forward.

title: Swizzle support is broken
author: zasdfgbnm
body: The swizzle support in our current system is very broken. There are more multiple bugs and workarounds, making it very hard to use. What is the correct behavior? A typical way to use swizzle is like below, for example, if we have T1_s[I2, I3] = set(T0[I0, I1]) T2[I4, I5] = set(T1_s[I2, I3]) we might do T1_s->split(1, s1); T1_s->split(0, s2); T1_s->swizzle(0, 2); T1_s->merge(0); T1_s->merge(1); we will get:  When indexing swizzle, we would like to generate code T1_s[swizzled_index] = T0[index] T2[index] = T1_s[swizzled_index] So, the desired behavior is:  When indexing T0, the producer of swizzled tensor, we should replay T0 as T1_s without replaying the swizzle, and index using backward traverse. When indexing T1_s as a consumer, we just use backward traverse regularly. When indexing T1_s as a producer, we should replay T1_s as T2 skipping swizzle. That is, we start from I2' and I3' pretending that they are the root domain of T1_s and stack T2's transformation on top of it. For example, if T2's leaf domain is I4*I5, then T1_s should be replayed as I2'*I3' instead of I2*I3.  Today, we now have allocation domain, so it is natural to implement swizzle using allocation domain, that is, make I2' and I3' the root domain, and I2, I3 the allocation domain. In the CA map we should have {I0, I2', I4} and {I1, I3', I5} exactly mapped together, but I2 and I3 should not be exactly mapped to I2' and I3'. Current status Honestly, I don't fully understand the current implementation of swizzle, but anything other than the above approach sound like a workaround. But I do observe some problems:  Swizzle is not indexed inside the backward traverse, but instead, there is a separate IndexSwizzle that hack the swizzle in after the original backward traverse. For the above case, BestEffortReplay can not skipped I2 as I2' and I3 as I3'. It can only skip I2o into I2o' and I3o into I3o', but it can not know that a split and merge-back yield the same ID. As a result, the CA map for tensor with swizzle is broken. The skip of swizzle in BestEffortReplay considers X and Y separately. For example, if you have the following schedule:  Because the inner split size of I2 and I4 is the same, we should have I4 mapped to I2, and I4o mapped to I2o. However, currently BestEffortReplay will skip swizzle and map I4o to I2o' instead of I2o, even though the matching I3o can not be mapped. For this case, if we replay T1_s as T2, we will get corrupted data in the replay.  Maybe related bug: #170 Due to these issues, swizzle in our system is pretty broken, and can can yield strange bugs, and it is pretty annoying to use it as observed when working on #387 (we initially started with an indexing error, we created a workaround for that indexing error, but we hit another error when tidy-up the implementation of the workaround). Moving forward, the only suggestion I have is to prioritize our indexing refactor, and abandon the whole current system entirely. I would like to make matmul an early adopter of the new indexing approach.

title: nvFuser's RNG agrees with PyTorch only on `(numel - 1) // 4 + 1` elements
author: IvanYashchuk
body: Am I correct that nvFuser and PyTorch use the same variant of Philox RNG? nvFuser also shares the RNG state with PyTorch so some users might expect the same values to be generated. Is this a reasonable expectation and something we can promise (as long as PyTorch keeps using the same generator as we do)? I tried exploring whether we're generating the same sequences as PyTorch, and we are not. But there's a pattern that the results match on the (total_number_of_elements - 1) // 4 + 1 number of elements. So for a size 1 tensor - 1 element is matching, size 5 -> 2 matches, size 9 -> 3 matches, size 13 -> 4 matches, and so on. What's going on here? Can we match PyTorch's behavior or can we make changes to PyTorch so that it matches nvFuser's behavior? Here's a script that I used: from nvfuser import FusionDefinition, DataType import torch from itertools import product  total_number_of_elements  = 423 shape = (total_number_of_elements ,) device = "cuda"  # Now let's try what sequence nvfuser will generate with FusionDefinition() as fd:     min = fd.define_scalar(0.0)     max = fd.define_scalar(1.0)     u = fd.ops.uniform(min, max, [fd.define_scalar(s) for s in shape])     fd.add_output(u)  # PyTorch Eager and nvFuser use different threading mapping so the position of # the elements in the output tensor will be different. However, the sorted values # can be the same. torch.manual_seed(0) pt_result = torch.rand(shape, device=device).ravel().sort().values  torch.manual_seed(0) nvfuser_result = fd.execute([])[0].ravel().sort().values  # count how many nvfuser elements are the same as the pytorch elements count = sum(x == y for x, y in product(pt_result, nvfuser_result)).item() print(f"nvfuser and pytorch agree on {count} elements out of {len(pt_result)}")

title: Segfault segmenting in presence of dangling unary Op chain from inputs
author: jacobhinkle
body: I encountered a segfault during segmentation when implementing #449 in SegmentCandidateFinder::forwardInputs() at https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/csrc/fusion_segmenter.cpp#L3408. That method tries to build a chain of UnaryOps from inputs, and implicitly assumes that there are uses for each output. This is triggered whenever we must segment (i.e. the complete Fusion cannot be scheduled) and there is a chain of UnaryOps from an input that eventually is unused. TEST_F(NVFuserTest, FusionDanglingUnaryOp_CUDA) {   auto fusion = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   FusionGuard fg(fusion.get());    // Create a segmented Fusion. We call segment_set here to ensure the whole   // Fusion cannot be scheduled. This triggers segmentation, so that   // forwardInputs() is called. The structure of this Fusion is not important;   // it is only important that it must be segmented.   auto size = IrBuilder::create<Scalar>(5);   auto tv0 = full({size}, fusion->zeroVal(), DataType::Int);   auto tv1 = segment_set(tv0);   fusion->addOutput(tv1);    // Now take in an input that has a chain of UnaryOp uses that terminates in a   // Val with no uses. This triggers a segfault in forwardInputs().   Val* alpha = IrBuilder::create<Scalar>(DataType::Int);   fusion->addInput(alpha);   neg(castOp(DataType::Float, alpha));    FusionExecutorCache executor_cache(std::move(fusion));    executor_cache.runFusionWithInputs({11}); }

title: Static pad to broadcast fails to schedule
author: jacobhinkle
body: This is a corner case for Resize ops that hasn't had a lot of attention yet, in which we use pad in a way that results in a broadcast that is then resolved. TEST_F(NVFuserTest, PadToBroadcast) {   auto fusion = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   FusionGuard fg(fusion.get());    auto tv0 = makeConcreteTensor({2});   auto tv1 = makeConcreteTensor({3});   fusion->addInput(tv0);   fusion->addInput(tv1);    auto tv2 = pad(tv0, {fusion->zeroVal(), IrBuilder::create<Scalar>(-1)});   auto tv3 = mul(tv1, tv2);   fusion->addOutput(tv3);    // Fusion is not dynamic   EXPECT_FALSE(fusion->hasDynamicTransform());    fusion->printMath();   /* Inputs:   T0_g[ iS0{2} ], float   T1_g[ iS1{3} ], float Outputs:   T3_g[ iS4{3} ], float                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           %kernel_math { T2_l[ bS3{1}rf ]    = pad( T0_g[ iS0{2} ], {0, -1} ) T3_g[ iS4{3} ]    = T1_g[ iS1{3} ]    * T2_l[ bS3{1}rf ]; }   */   auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);    auto t0 = at::randn({2}, options);   auto t1 = at::randn({3}, options);   std::vector<c10::IValue> aten_inputs({t0, t1});    auto args = KernelArgumentHolder::createKernelArgumentHolder(aten_inputs);   FusionKernelRuntime runtime(std::move(fusion), args);   /* terminate called after throwing an instance of 'c10::Error'   what():  it != broadcast_origin_map_.end() INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/device_lower/analysis/trivial_broadcast.cpp":98, please report a bug to PyTorch. Broadcast origin info not found for producer broadcast domain: bS3{1}rf of T2_l[ bS3{1}rf ] Exception raised from handle at /opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/device_lower/analysis/trivial_broadcast.cpp:98 (most recent call first)   */    runtime.compileFusionParallel(args);   auto cg_outputs = runtime.runWithInputs(args);    auto t2_padded = at::pad(t0, {0, -1});   auto ref_t2 = t1 * t2_padded;    testValidate(       runtime.fusionSegments()->completeFusion(),       cg_outputs,       aten_inputs,       {ref_t2},       __LINE__,       __FILE__); } Simply determining the output IterType is not sufficient to be able to actually resolve the broadcast. We instead need to have an actual tensor allocated to act as the broadcast origin. This can be done in this case by translating the pad to   auto tv2 = broadcast(select(tv0, 0, fusion->zeroVal()), {true}); in which case select introduces the needed intermediate tensor which is the origin of the following broadcast. Note that dynamic pad faces a similar issue but that we should probably fix this static case first. Static and dynamic slice will face a similar problem (related to #511).

body: There is an issue with computing the output shape in some cases with broadcast_in_dim: from nvfuser import DataType, FusionDefinition import torch from torch.testing import make_tensor  a = make_tensor((1, 0), device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)  with FusionDefinition() as fd:     T0 = fd.define_tensor(symbolic_sizes=[1, -1], contiguity=[None, True], dtype=DataType.Float, is_cpu=False)     T1 = fd.ops.broadcast_in_dim(T0, output_shape=[0, 0], broadcast_dims=[0, 1])     fd.add_output(T1)  nvfout, = fd.execute([a])  # This fails because nvfout.shape is (1, 0) assert nvfout.shape == torch.Size((0, 0)) The Fusion seems to be constructed properly: Inputs:   T0_g[ bS0{1}, iS1{i1} ], float Outputs:   T2_g[ bS4{0}, iS5{i1} ], float  %kernel_math { T1_l[ bS2{1}, iS3{i1} ]    = Set( T0_g[ bS0{1}, iS1{i1} ] ) T2_g[ bS4{0}, iS5{i1} ] = expand( T1_l[ bS2{1}, iS3{i1} ], {0, i1} ) }  Note that changing the first dimension of a to 0 and setting symbolic_sizes=[-1,-1], contiguity=[True,True] gives us the correct behavior. The issue seems to be in expanding to zero size. This might be an issue with the remove empty pass checking extent instead of getMaybeExpandedExtent.

title: Dependency on NCCL/UCC is implicit in the build
author: jjsjann123
body: With our recent added support in distributed primitives, we introduced dependency against NCCL/UCC in our code base. https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/tree/main/csrc/multidevice                Fuser/CMakeLists.txt                   Lines 140 to 144       in       fb9845e                                                 ${NVFUSER_SRCS_DIR}/multidevice/communicator.cpp                                           ${NVFUSER_SRCS_DIR}/multidevice/executor.cpp                                           ${NVFUSER_SRCS_DIR}/multidevice/runtime.cpp                                           ${NVFUSER_SRCS_DIR}/multidevice/pipeline.cpp                                           ${NVFUSER_SRCS_DIR}/multidevice/pipeline_ir.cpp                     This part is not well tested against various build of pytorch (pytorch build with USE_DISTRIBUTED=0 have been causing issue: i.e. #598 (comment)). More over, the dependency on NCCL/UCC is currently required I believe. Which arguably isn't necessary. A couple actionable items:  We should have our source and build file better organized and allow build like USE_MULTIDEVICE=0 to avoid dependency on NCCL/UCC and future libraries required for multi device support. Explicit documentation in the build guide and refactor on build system to allow easy installation of dependencies.

title: Generalize ReductionOp to support argmax and online softmax
author: jacobhinkle
body: This is a proposal to refactor reductions in nvfuser in order to support argmin and argmax, unifying them with Welford. I believe we can do this in a way that will let us implement online softmax and other efficient methods conveniently. Current status We currently implement Min and Max binary operations which can appear as the reduction op in a ReductionOp, over any number of axes. This is what our min and max ops do, using an initial value of plus or minus infinity, respectively. In PyTorch, torch.amax works like our max, and torch.max returns both the max and the argmax. Note that torch.amax can reduce along multiple dimensions, but torch.max works on either a single dimension, or on the flattened input. This is needed since it is ambiguous how one would compute a linear index when reducing multiple dimensions; is it the linear index in the entire tensor or only in the reduced dims? Proposed approach I propose that we generalize GroupedReductionOp to MultiReductionOp. This would represent an arbitrary reduction over the concatenation of M tensors, producing N reduced values each of which might depend on all of the M tensors. All M tensors and N aggregated values can have different dtypes. Here is a sketch of the interface: //! Describes the types of multi-reductions we could do enum class MultiReductionBinaryOpType {   ArgMin,   ArgMax,   Welford,   Independent // simple ReductionOp or GroupedReductionOp };  //! Describes a MultiReductionOp without the axis or input info class MultiReductionOpType {   MultiReductionBinaryOpType getOpType() const;    //! How many aggregated values (output tensors) will we create?   int getNumAggregateValues() const;   //! Initialize the aggregate values according to the op type   std::vector<Val*> getDefaultInitValues() const;   std::vector<DataType>& getAggregateDataTypes() const;    //! How many TensorViews are expected and what are their dtypes?   int getNumTensorArgs() const;   std::vector<DataType>& getTensorDataTypes() const;    //! If this is an Independent, get the binary ops   std::vector<BinaryOp> getGroupedBinaryOps() const;   // ... };  class MultiReductionOp : public Expr {   MultiReductionOp(       MultiReductionOpType op_type,       std::vector<TensorView*> tvs,       std::vector<int64_t> axes);   // ... }; A simple ReductionOp is a case where M=N=1 and the dtypes are equal; getGroupedBinaryOps() would return the usual BinaryOp. Special case: argmax We can pass two tensors to argmax: the input A and an index tensor idx, which we could create using iota. if (A[i] > m[i-1]) {   m[i] = A[i];   x[i] = idx[i]; } else {   m[i] = m[i-1];   x[i] = x[i-1]; } This results in m[N] the max and x[N] the first corresponding entry in idx. We would initialize m with -inf and x with 0 (although this is arbitrary). Special case: WelfordOp Welford can be easily expressed this way: n[i] = n[i-1] + 1 avg[i] = avg[i-1] + (A[i] - avg[i-1]) / n[i] var_sum[i] = var_sum[i-1] + (A[i] - avg[i-1]) * (A[i] - avg[i])  Notice that unlike argmax this only needs a single tensor input, so M=1, N=3 in the notation of MultiReductionOp. The aggregate values have initial values (0, 0,0) and dtypes Int, Float, Float. Note that in order to use with rfactor, this is generalized to use a count for each A[i] instead of 1, in which case we would likely rewrite this to take M=3 tensors, two of which are initialized to 1 and 0. Special case: Online softmax In softmax, we need to convert each tensor element A[i] to exp(A[i])/sum(exp(A[i])). A naive implementation like this quickly results in floating point overflow for large values of A[i]. Instead, the more stable implementation of softmax is m = max(A[i]) softmax[i] = exp(A[i] - m) / sum(exp(A[i] - m))  This requires two successive reductions: max followed by sum. The online softmax algorithm fuses the two reductions into a single two-way reduction: m[i] = max(m[i-1], A[i]) d[i] = d[i-1] * exp(m[i-1] - m[i]) + exp(A[i] - m[i])  At the end of the reduction, m[N] is the overall max of A and d[i] is the sum(exp(A[i] - m)) normalization term. The softmax is then formed by computing softmax[i] = exp(A[i] - m[N]) / d[N]  The normalization term is simple to implement as an 2-way reduction op, very similar to how we would implement argmin and argmax. If we implement this op, we could insert it in an optimization pass by pattern matching for the sumexp pattern. For an implementation in CUDA, see https://github.com/NVIDIA/online-softmax and the manuscript Mikalov & Gimelshein 2018. Special case: Flash attention Flash attention takes the fusion from online softmax and goes further. In dot-product attention, softmax surrounded by matmul operations, the second of which contracts along the softmax dimension. This contraction is another reduction which flash attention fuses to the online softmax. Flash attention also does tiling, so that the first matmul and fused second matmul can operate on individual tiles; that is outside the scope of this PR. However, being able to express N-Way reductions opens the door to some day fusing them with the sum in a matmul. See Dao et al. 2022 for more info on flash attention. Challenges/Questions  Like GroupedReductionOp, MultiReductionOp should take variable numbers of aggregate values and tensors. The number of needed aggregate values and tensors is determined by the op type. It may be difficult to write the CUDA helper templates without specializing for each op type. There is a lot of code in scheduling and lowering specializing on reductions that will require careful adaptation. We should keep that all in place while initially developing MultiReductionOp separately with only argmin and argmax then replacing WelfordOp if this approach is successful. Currently I believe GroupedReductionOp and GroupedWelfordOp are meant for only grid persistent reductions, while MultiReductionOp should work for any size and memory location. I don't know yet if there will be a challenge in supporting both with the same class. If not, we can keep the grouped versions separate indefinitely. Enumerating all the patterns for reduction is a bit cumbersome considering we have a rich system in place for describing arbitrary expressions already. Instead of ArgMin and ArgMax, could we instead just hold a collection of Vals describing outputs whose definitions relate them all to inputs which are grouped into old_aggregates and new_tensor_vals? That would let us very easily add new reduction types. For example, Welford might be defined like this:  // create constant Vals to initialize aggregates std::vector<Val*> init_vals = {     container->zeroVal(DataType::Int),     container->zeroVal(DataType::Float),     container->zeroVal(DataType::Float), };  // create placeholder Vals for each previous aggregate value auto n_prev = IrBuilder::create<Scalar>(DataType::Int); auto avg_prev = IrBuilder::create<Scalar>(DataType::Float); auto var_sum_prev = IrBuilder::create<Scalar>(DataType::Float); std::vector<Val*> old_aggregates = {n_prev, avg_prev, var_sum_prev};  // create placeholder Vals for each new tensor input value auto a_i = IrBuilder::create<Scalar>(DataType::Float); std::vector<Val*> new_tensor_vals = {a_i};  // Now define the actual op using Exprs auto n = add(n_prev, container->oneVal()); // can easily generalize to the count of a_i instead of 1 auto diff_prev = sub(a_i, avg_prev); // Note we can explicitly CSE here auto avg = add(avg_prev, div(diff_prev, n)); auto diff_next = sub(a_i, avg); auto var_sum = add(var_sum_prev, mul(diff_prev, diff_next));  // Output is the collection of new aggregate values std::vector<Val*> new_aggregates = {n, avg, var_sum};  // Create the op with these flexible val lists instead of (or in addition to) an enumerated op type IrBuilder::create<MultiReductionOp>(     container,     out_tensors, // one newForReduction for each of new_aggregates, with corresponding dtype     {input_tensor},     init_vals,     old_aggregates,     new_tensor_vals,     new_aggregates); ### Tasks - [ ] Implement `MultiReductionOp` with `MinWithArg` and `MaxWithArg` op types - [ ] Update python bindings for `min` and `max` to enable access to arg versions - [ ] Make `WelfordOp` a special case of `MultiReductionOp` - [ ] Implement online softmax

title: Issues/TODOs related to pipeline parallelism and multidevice support
author: samnordmann
body: Here is a list of issues/todos related to pipeline parallelism and multidevice support. Most of these points come from comments on this PR #483 Multidevice support:   Implement multi node support. For now we only support devices on the same node  Implement asynchronous non-blocking collective communications. For now, the only communications are blocking p2p send receive (we wait for completion right after posting the operation)  #639  add multidevice tests in CI.  measure performance of collectives  Pipeline/task parallelism    Separate the pipeline logic and the multidevice support. The pipeline parallelism (or task parallelism) can be reused for other applications.  class PipelineStage and PipelineVal and PipelineCommunication, maybe also PipelinePrinter, should be in ir/ directory ir/ directory should be self contained, and should not have dependency on multidevice/ directory discussion1, discussion2     Make partition of DAG hierarchical/composable/recursive. Design and implement an interface to partition a DAG into subgraphs with different level of granularity, without assuming how these partition will be used. Build out utilities for operating on these partitions. discussion  Make the partitionning deeply integrated into fusion definition. The pipeline descriptor should be owned by the fusion, and not be a separate thing sitting on the side, as in the current implementation. For example, we should be able to do val->getPipelineStage() , val->addToPipelineStage(...), val1->getPipelineStage()->mergeWith(val2->getPipelineStage()), etc. for a Val*. discussion1 discussion2  Communicator   we need to think about how/where to instantiate a communicator in nvFuser, and what we expect from the user in the front-end. Since we get WORLD_SIZE from the communicator, it might be used even at the scheduling step #797 (comment)  test UCC, GLOO and MPI ProcessGroup's backends. Only NCCL has been tested for now  Link with UCC, and/or openmpi. Maybe also NVshmem. Dockerize.  Build/linkage  make a separate library to hide all dependencies on gloo, ucc, nccl, etc., so that nvfuser could just link to this separate library. #797 (comment)  Utility functions    Reimplement the Pipeline’s method: /* returns a Fusion copied from the originalFusion but            with I/O as the stage's I/O */       std::unique_ptr<Fusion> Pipeline::stageToFusion(PipelineStage*& stage) const For now, we copy entirely the original fusion and then only change the inputs and outputs. It should be optimized by copying only the IRs needed for the traversal between the stage’s I/O.    (see discussion) Implement a function std::vector<shape_type> inferShape(   std::vector<Val*> target_vals,   const std::vector<shape_type> inputs,    Fusion* fusion) that infer the shape for some vals target_vals given a fusion and some concrete inputs. shape_type is whatever type is usually used for shapes. This utility function would be used in the multidevice executor for allocating recv buffers when receiving tensors from other devices (these tensors are outputs of the previous stage and inputs of the next stage). What we do for now, is simply to allocate buffers for every inputs/outputs for every stage, which makes a lot of garbage allocation. Moreover, the allocation space is computed by running the fusion, through the following function (in csrc/kernel_cache.h ) //! Allocate the outputs of the Fusion given inputs //! TODO: re-implement std::vector<at::Tensor> FusionExecutorCache::allocOutputSpace(    const at::ArrayRef<c10::IValue>& inputs) {       return runFusionWithInputs(inputs); } This causes garbage computation.    add a function void PipelineStageDescriptor::addRange(Val* start, Val* end, Fusion* fusion) to add to a Pipeline Stage a range of a fusion (defined by the DAG traversal between start and end) rather than adding the Vals one by one as is currently done with the method void void addVal(std::vector<Val*> vals)

title: Extent root scalars can get lost during segmentation
author: jacobhinkle
body: In fixing #418 I encountered this segmentation error. First, the offending test TEST_F(NVFuserTest, DynamicTransformIssue418_CUDA) {   auto fusion = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   FusionGuard fg(fusion.get());    auto tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(4);   fusion->addInput(tv0);   auto s0 = IrBuilder::create<Val>(DataType::Int);   fusion->addInput(s0);    auto sh = tensor_sizes(tv0);   auto tv1 = reshape(tv0, {sh[0], div(sh[1], s0), s0, sh[2], sh[3]});   // Reducing along axis 2 in tv1 is equivalent to a partial reduction across   // axis 1 of tv0.   auto vm = variance_mean(tv1, {2, 3, 4}, 0, true);   fusion->addOutput(vm.mean);   fusion->addOutput(vm.var);    FusionExecutorCache fusion_executor_cache(std::move(fusion));    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   at::Tensor at0 = at::randn({256, 128, 28, 28}, options);   std::vector<c10::IValue> aten_inputs = {at0, 32};   auto outputs = fusion_executor_cache.runFusionWithInputs(aten_inputs);   /* Concretized Fusion: Inputs:   T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2}, iS2{i3}, iS3{i4} ], float   i5, int64_t Outputs:   T7_g[ iS49{i0}, iS50{( i2 / i5 )}, bS37{1}, bS38{1}, bS39{1} ], float   T6_g[ iS55{i0}, iS56{( i2 / i5 )}, bS32{1}, bS33{1}, bS34{1} ], float %kernel_math { T8_l[ iS40{i0}, iS45{4}rf, iS46{( ceilDiv(i2, 4) )}rf, iS42{i3}, iS43{i4} ]   = view( T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2}, iS2{i3}, iS3{i4} ] ) T2_l[ iS47{i0}, iS48{( i2 / i5 )}, rS15{i5}, rS16{i3}, rS17{i4} ](Avg), T3_l[ iS51{i0}, iS52{( i2 / i5 )}, rS20{i5}, rS21{i3}, rS22{i4} ](Var), T4_l[ iS57{i0}, iS58{( i2 / i5 )}, rS25{i5}, rS26{i3}, rS27{i4} ](Count)  = Welford ( T8_l[ iS40{i0}, iS45{4}rf, iS46{( ceilDiv(i2, 4) )}rf, iS42{i3}, iS43{i4} ](Avg),   allreduce = false ) T7_g[ iS49{i0}, iS50{( i2 / i5 )}, bS37{1}, bS38{1}, bS39{1} ]   = broadcast( T2_l[ iS47{i0}, iS48{( i2 / i5 )}, rS15{i5}, rS16{i3}, rS17{i4} ] ) d17 = (double)(i5); d19 = double(1) * d17; d21 = (double)(i3); d23 = d19 * d21; d25 = (double)(i4); d27 = d23 * d25; d33 = reciprocal(d27); T5_l[ iS53{i0}, iS54{( i2 / i5 )} ]   = T3_l[ iS51{i0}, iS52{( i2 / i5 )}, rS20{i5}, rS21{i3}, rS22{i4} ]   * d33; T6_g[ iS55{i0}, iS56{( i2 / i5 )}, bS32{1}, bS33{1}, bS34{1} ]   = broadcast( T5_l[ iS53{i0}, iS54{( i2 / i5 )} ] ) }   */   /*   what():  inferred_val.hasValue() INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/executor.cpp":477,  please report a bug to PyTorch. Could not launch kernel as program could not infer  ( i2 / i5 )(i6) for the buffer T7_g[ iS49{i0}, iS50{( i2 / i5 )}, bS37{1}, bS38{1}, bS39{1} ] Exception raised from inferShape at /opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/executor.cpp:477 (most recent call first):   */   auto at1 = at0.reshape({256, 4, 32, 28, 28});   auto atmean = at1.mean({2, 3, 4});   auto atvar = at1.var({2, 3, 4});   testValidate(       fusion_executor_cache.fusion(),       outputs,       aten_inputs,       {atmean, atvar},       __LINE__,       __FILE__); } This error occurs because the Fusion is segmented at tv1 (printed as T8_l[ iS40{i0}, iS45{4}rf, iS46{( ceilDiv(i2, 4) )}rf, iS42{i3}, iS43{i4} ]), since there is a split axis with a reduction along only one branch of the split. In the second segment, that tensor is an input, along with the scalars used to compute T5: i3, i4, i5. However, i2 is not an input so it can't evaluate the extent, even though it is actually provided as an input. We could either attempt to add missing input scalars to fusion segments so that each segment will have all inputs necessary to compute any extent expressions contained in that segment, or we could modify bindInputs to be able to bind values to derived extents like i2 / i5, so that that extent would be available directly in the ExpressionEvaluator.

title: `keepdim=False` then `broadcast_in_dim` removes explicit alias registers and shared memory can't be reused.
author: liqiangxl
body: When working on #582 and test softmax, I found that if FusionDefinition use keepdim=False then broadcast_in_dim, the generated code failed to explicitly use alias registers. There is no influence on performance since the compiler can auto reuse. But this disables shared memory reuse when the register buffers are changed to shared memroy buffers in #582 . title: Missing optimization when fusion definition is using div(a,b) instead of mul(a,reciprocal(b))
author: liqiangxl
body: When benchmarking softmax noticed about 10% performance drop if fusion definition is using div(a,b) instead of mul(a,reciprocal(b)) . The mul version avoided multiple div ops in a for-loop. import torch from nvfuser import FusionDefinition, DataType  def nvfuser_fusion_id0(fd : FusionDefinition) -> None :     T0 = fd.define_tensor(symbolic_sizes=[-1, -1], contiguity=[True, True], dtype=DataType.Half, is_cpu=False)     T1 = fd.ops.cast(T0, dtype=DataType.Float)     T2 = fd.ops.max(T1, axes=[1], keepdim=True, dtype=DataType.Null)     T5 = fd.ops.sub(T1, T2)     T6 = fd.ops.exp(T5)     T7 = fd.ops.sum(T6, axes=[1], keepdim=True, dtype=DataType.Null)     T10 = fd.ops.div(T6, T7)     T11 = fd.ops.cast(T10, dtype=DataType.Half)     fd.add_output(T11)  with FusionDefinition() as fd:     nvfuser_fusion_id0(fd)  inputs = [     torch.randn((8192, 10240), dtype=torch.float16, device='cuda:0').as_strided((8192, 10240), (10240, 1)), ] fd.execute(inputs)  Optimized should be:   T8 = fd.ops.reciprocal(T7)     T10 = fd.ops.mul(T6, T8)

title: Cleanup legacy methods in `Val`
author: zasdfgbnm
body: Current, Val has the following methods:   // If this Val is an integer with a direct constant value associated with it,   // will return the value of that constant integer. If this integer has   // defining expressions it will return a std::nullopt. Those values should be   // infered using evaluateInt.   std::optional<int64_t> getInt() const;    // If this Val is a double with a direct constant value associated with it,   // will return the value of that constant double. If this double has   // defining expressions it will return a std::nullopt. Those values should be   // infered using evaluateDouble.   std::optional<double> getDouble() const;    // If this Val is a bool with a direct constant value associated with it,   // will return the value of that constant bool. If this bool has defining   // expressions it will return a std::nullopt. Those values should be infered   // using evaluateBool.   std::optional<bool> getBool() const;    // If this Val is a constant integer, and its history is comprised only of   // constant values, will return the value of that constant integer. Cannot   // make constant as expression evaluator takes non-constant Vals.   int64_t evaluateInt();    // If this Val is a constant double, and its history is comprised only of   // constant values, will return the value of that constant double. Cannot   // make constant as expression evaluator takes non-constant Vals.   double evaluateDouble();    // If this Val is a constant bool, and its history is comprised only of   // constant values, will return the value of that constant bool. Cannot   // make constant as expression evaluator takes non-constant Vals.   bool evaluateBool(); This was a legacy before we have a PolymorphicValue. With PolymorphicValue, we only need a single const PolymorphicValue& value() const; and a single PolymorphicValue evaluate(); we should replace all uses of the above 6 legacy methods with the two new methods.

title: More lost scalars during segmentation for dynamic reshape
author: jacobhinkle
body: // Test concretizing a pad that follows a reshape. This requires the // ExpressionEvaluator used in concretization to propagate shapes properly // across symbolic reshapes in order to infer the size of the downstream pad. TEST_F(NVFuserTest, DynamicReshapePad_CUDA) {   std::unique_ptr<Fusion> fusion_ptr = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   Fusion& fusion = *fusion_ptr.get();   FusionGuard fg(&fusion);    TensorView* tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(2);    /* Symbolic Fusion: Inputs:   T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ], float   i3, int64_t   i4, int64_t   i5, int64_t   i6, int64_t Outputs:   T2_g[ ?S7{( i5 + i4 )}rf, ?S9{( i6 + i3 )}rf ], float  %kernel_math { T1_l[ ?S4{i5}rf, ?S5{i6}rf ] = view( T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ] ) T2_g[ ?S7{( i5 + i4 )}rf, ?S9{( i6 + i3 )}rf ]    = pad( T1_l[ ?S4{i5}rf, ?S5{i6}rf ], {0, i4, 0, i3} ) }  Concretized Fusion: Inputs:   T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ], float   i3, int64_t   i4, int64_t   i5, int64_t   i6, int64_t Outputs:   T2_g[ iS21{( i5 + i4 )}rf, iS22{( i6 + i3 )}rf ], float  %kernel_math { T3_l[ iS15{3}rf, iS16{( ceilDiv(( i0 * i2 ), 3) )}rf ] = view( T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ] ) T2_g[ iS21{( i5 + i4 )}rf, iS22{( i6 + i3 )}rf ]    = pad( T3_l[ iS15{3}rf, iS16{( ceilDiv(( i0 * i2 ), 3) )}rf ], {0, i4, 0, i3} ) }  T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2} ]  root domain : (iS0{i0}, iS1{i2})  contiguity: f f  leaf domain : (iS0{i0}, iS1{i2}) T3_l[ iS15{3}rf, iS16{( ceilDiv(( i0 * i2 ), 3) )}rf ]  root domain : (iS12{i0}rf, iS13{i2}rf)   Merge: iS12{i0}rf and iS13{i2}rf -> iS14{( i0 * i2 )}rf   Outer split: iS14{( i0 * i2 )}rf by factor 3 -> iS15{3}rf, iS16{( ceilDiv(( i0 * i2 ), 3) )}rf, start offset: 0, stop offset: 0  rfactor domain : (iS15{3}rf, iS16{( ceilDiv(( i0 * i2 ), 3) )}rf)  contiguity: t t  leaf domain : (iS15{3}rf, iS16{( ceilDiv(( i0 * i2 ), 3) )}rf) T2_g[ iS21{( i5 + i4 )}rf, iS22{( i6 + i3 )}rf ]  root domain : (iS19{i5}rf, iS20{i6}rf)   Resize: iS19{i5}rf by 0 and i4 -> iS21{( i5 + i4 )}rf   Resize: iS20{i6}rf by 0 and i3 -> iS22{( i6 + i3 )}rf  rfactor domain : (iS21{( i5 + i4 )}rf, iS22{( i6 + i3 )}rf)  contiguity: t t  leaf domain : (iS21{( i5 + i4 )}rf, iS22{( i6 + i3 )}rf)   */    FusionExecutorCache fusion_executor_cache(std::move(fusion_ptr));    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   at::Tensor at_x = at::randn({4, 3}, options);   std::vector<c10::IValue> aten_inputs = {at_x, 1, 1, 3, 4};   auto at_y = at::pad(at_x.reshape({3, 4}), {0, 1, 0, 1});    auto outputs = fusion_executor_cache.runFusionWithInputs(aten_inputs);   /* terminate called after throwing an instance of 'c10::Error'   what():  val.hasValue() INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/executor.cpp":1039, please report a bug to PyTorch. Tried to evaluate the extent, ( ceilDiv(( ( ( ( i5 * i6 ) + ( i5 * i3 ) ) + ( i4 * i6 ) ) + ( i4 * i3 ) ), 128) )  for the ptype: blockIdx.x to set launch bounds but could not.   */    testValidate(       fusion_executor_cache.fusion(),       outputs,       aten_inputs,       {at_y},       __LINE__,       __FILE__); } The fusion gets segmented at T3 and the second segment cannot evaluate the output extent, just like in #629. The fix in that case (#630) was to propagate the replaced extents during concretization. In this case that approach does not resolve the issue, since the downstream pad op builds an extent expression using the fusion inputs i5 and i6. Although we register those values for mutation, the actual rfactor extents in T2 are i5 + i4 and i6 + i3 so they are not replaced. It is not necessarily clear that replacing them before segmentation is always advantageous either: before segmentation we don't know if the original expression with fusion inputs, e.g. i6 + i3, will be easier to compute than the concretized one: ceilDiv(( i0 * i2), 3) + i3.

title: Vectorization failure with reduction domains in fusion inputs
author: naoyam
body: Found while cleaning up the vectorization helper (#654). See #654 (comment) In NVFuserTest.FusionSegmentReduceSoftmax_CUDA, the fusion has a standard reduction followed by a softmax. It's a test to exercise segmentation such that the first reduction comprises a first segment and the softmax does a second segment. The issue is that we fail to vectorize the second softmax kernel even though the problem size is large enough and all inputs and outputs are contiguous.
