title: Replace `TORCH_CHECK` and `TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT` Macros
author: kevinstephano
body: TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT asks the user to report errors to Pytorch which no longer makes sense.  Additionally, it would be nice if the macros automatically gave a function signature and line number in a file so the user can find the error faster. One example where that would be nice is in arith.cpp for the size() function where the user manually adds the __FUNCTION__ macro. Val* size(TensorView* inp, int64_t dim) {   auto iter_domains = TensorDomain::noReductions(inp->getMaybeRFactorDomain());   auto idx = dim;   if (idx < 0) {     idx = static_cast<int64_t>(iter_domains.size()) + idx;   }   TORCH_CHECK(       (idx >= 0) && (static_cast<size_t>(idx) < iter_domains.size()),       __FUNCTION__,       ": The dimension requested is beyond the bounds of the shape of the indexed tensor!",       " Tensor Dims: ",       iter_domains.size(),       " Dim: ",       dim);   return iter_domains.at(idx)->getMaybeExpandedExtent(); }

title: Build out `Expr::evaluate` for operators, and clean up unit tests
author: zasdfgbnm
body: During the nvFuser development process, one of our routine tasks is to create a fusion and then compare the output of our codegen with the ATen version of the fusion. Manually writing an ATen implementation can be both challenging and time-consuming. As an example, the test provided below requires 23 lines of carefully constructed ATen code: // extracted from NVFuserTest.FusionLayerNormFusedOpsRedundantCast_CUDA TEST_F(NVFuserTest, ExampleTest) {   std::unique_ptr<Fusion> fusion_ptr = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   auto fusion = fusion_ptr.get();   FusionGuard fg(fusion);    const float kEps = 1e-5;   const int batch_size = 2048 * 8;   const int hidden_size = 20480;   {     DataType dtype = DataType::Half;     auto tv0 = makeContigTensor(1, dtype);     auto tv1 = makeContigTensor(2, dtype);     auto tv2 = makeContigTensor(1, dtype);     auto tv3 = makeContigTensor(1, dtype);     auto tv4 = makeContigTensor(1, dtype);      fusion->addInput(tv0);     fusion->addInput(tv1);     fusion->addInput(tv2);     fusion->addInput(tv3);     fusion->addInput(tv4);     auto tv5 = broadcast(tv0, {true, false});     auto tv6 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv1);     auto tv7 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv5);     auto tv8 = add(tv6, tv7);     auto tv9 = castOp(DataType::Half, tv8);     auto tv10 = broadcast(tv2, {true, false});     auto tv11 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv9);     auto tv12 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv10);     auto tv13 = add(tv11, tv12);     auto tv14 = castOp(DataType::Half, tv13);     auto tv15 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv14);     auto tv16 = variance(tv15, {1}, false, false);     auto tv17 = broadcast(tv16, {false, true});     auto tv18 = sum(tv15, {1}, false);     auto tv19 = broadcast(tv18, {false, true});      nvfuser::Val* num_features = IrBuilder::create<Val>(1.0);     num_features = mul(num_features, tv0->getLeafDomain()[0]->extent());     auto s20 = num_features;      auto s21 = reciprocal(s20);     auto tv22 = mul(tv19, s21);     auto s23 = IrBuilder::create<Val>(kEps);     auto tv24 = add(tv17, s23);     auto tv25 = rsqrt(tv24);     auto tv26 = broadcast(tv22, {false, false});     auto tv27 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv14);     auto tv28 = sub(tv27, tv26);     auto tv29 = broadcast(tv25, {false, false});     auto tv30 = mul(tv28, tv29);     auto tv31 = broadcast(tv4, {true, false});     auto tv32 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv31);     auto tv33 = mul(tv30, tv32);     auto tv34 = broadcast(tv3, {true, false});     auto tv35 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv34);     auto tv36 = add(tv33, tv35);     auto tv37 = castOp(DataType::Half, tv36);     fusion->addOutput(tv37);   }    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kHalf).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   std::vector<c10::IValue> inputs;   std::vector<at::Tensor> outputs;    {     auto t0 = at::randn({hidden_size}, options);     auto t1 = at::randn({batch_size, hidden_size}, options);     auto t2 = at::randn({hidden_size}, options);     auto t3 = at::randn({hidden_size}, options);     auto t4 = at::randn({hidden_size}, options);     inputs.emplace_back(t0);     inputs.emplace_back(t1);     inputs.emplace_back(t2);     inputs.emplace_back(t3);     inputs.emplace_back(t4);     auto t5 = t0.unsqueeze(0).expand({batch_size, hidden_size});     auto t6 = t1.to(at::kFloat);     auto t7 = t5.to(at::kFloat);     auto t8 = at::add(t6, t7);     auto t9 = t8.to(at::kHalf);     auto t10 = t2.unsqueeze(0).expand({batch_size, hidden_size});     auto t11 = t9.to(at::kFloat);     auto t12 = t10.to(at::kFloat);     auto t13 = at::add(t11, t12);     auto t14 = t13.to(at::kHalf);     auto aten_outputs = at::native_layer_norm(t14, {hidden_size}, t4, t3, kEps);     auto t33 = std::get<0>(aten_outputs);     outputs.emplace_back(t33);   }    FusionExecutorCache fec(std::move(fusion_ptr));   auto cg_outputs = fec.runFusionWithInputs(inputs);   testValidate(fusion, cg_outputs, inputs, outputs, __LINE__, __FILE__); } Errors can easily occur when creating these implementations by hand, which can cause confusion during the debugging stage. For instance, if an incorrect ATen reference is used, causing a mismatch in your testValidate, you may mistakenly assume this is due to a bug in the codegen. This could lead to unnecessary time spent debugging the codegen. We have developed a tool that automates the process of building ATen implementations. It can be found at https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/tools/cpp-repro-gen.py. However, this tool's output often requires manual adjustments to be functional. For example, it might create at::gather as the ATen reference code for nvfuser::gather, even though these two are completely separate things. They just happen to share the same name. To make the ATen code generated by cpp-repro-gen.py more usable, we would need to create a detailed pattern matching system for our fusion definitions and develop rules for converting them into ATen. The main issue with cpp-repro-gen.py is that it acts like a mini-compiler. It takes the python fusion definition as a string, then translates this string into a C++ fusion definition and an ATen implementation as output. Since we don't currently have a stable API and IR definition, cpp-repro-gen.py may require updates whenever we modify our IR node definition. In general, we don't see cpp-repro-gen.py as a long-term solution for improving debuggability, and it isn't a good use of our time to keep refining cpp-repro-gen.py. Recently, we incorporated a new class, PolymorphicValue, capable of storing data of various types such as int64_t, double, at::Tensor, etc. We also expanded our ExpressionEvaluator to handle all these data types. This enhancement allows us to contemplate the creation of an ATen backend for nvFuser IR, which can be evaluated by ExpressionEvaluator. To achieve this, we need to override the Expr::evaluate method for subclasses of Expr. If the evaluate method is overridden for all expressions in the fusion definition, then we can omit the ATen reference in testValidate. Consequently, testValidate will automatically utilize the ExpressionEvaluator to compute the ATen reference. An excellent example of how to override Expr::evaluate and clean up tests is provided in #575. For the NVFuserTest.ExampleTest example above, after the cleanup, the code should resemble: // extracted from NVFuserTest.FusionLayerNormFusedOpsRedundantCast_CUDA TEST_F(NVFuserTest, ExampleTest) {   std::unique_ptr<Fusion> fusion_ptr = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   auto fusion = fusion_ptr.get();   FusionGuard fg(fusion);    const float kEps = 1e-5;   const int batch_size = 2048 * 8;   const int hidden_size = 20480;   {     DataType dtype = DataType::Half;     auto tv0 = makeContigTensor(1, dtype);     auto tv1 = makeContigTensor(2, dtype);     auto tv2 = makeContigTensor(1, dtype);     auto tv3 = makeContigTensor(1, dtype);     auto tv4 = makeContigTensor(1, dtype);      fusion->addInput(tv0);     fusion->addInput(tv1);     fusion->addInput(tv2);     fusion->addInput(tv3);     fusion->addInput(tv4);     auto tv5 = broadcast(tv0, {true, false});     auto tv6 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv1);     auto tv7 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv5);     auto tv8 = add(tv6, tv7);     auto tv9 = castOp(DataType::Half, tv8);     auto tv10 = broadcast(tv2, {true, false});     auto tv11 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv9);     auto tv12 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv10);     auto tv13 = add(tv11, tv12);     auto tv14 = castOp(DataType::Half, tv13);     auto tv15 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv14);     auto tv16 = variance(tv15, {1}, false, false);     auto tv17 = broadcast(tv16, {false, true});     auto tv18 = sum(tv15, {1}, false);     auto tv19 = broadcast(tv18, {false, true});      nvfuser::Val* num_features = IrBuilder::create<Val>(1.0);     num_features = mul(num_features, tv0->getLeafDomain()[0]->extent());     auto s20 = num_features;      auto s21 = reciprocal(s20);     auto tv22 = mul(tv19, s21);     auto s23 = IrBuilder::create<Val>(kEps);     auto tv24 = add(tv17, s23);     auto tv25 = rsqrt(tv24);     auto tv26 = broadcast(tv22, {false, false});     auto tv27 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv14);     auto tv28 = sub(tv27, tv26);     auto tv29 = broadcast(tv25, {false, false});     auto tv30 = mul(tv28, tv29);     auto tv31 = broadcast(tv4, {true, false});     auto tv32 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv31);     auto tv33 = mul(tv30, tv32);     auto tv34 = broadcast(tv3, {true, false});     auto tv35 = castOp(DataType::Float, tv34);     auto tv36 = add(tv33, tv35);     auto tv37 = castOp(DataType::Half, tv36);     fusion->addOutput(tv37);   }    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kHalf).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   auto t0 = at::randn({hidden_size}, options);   auto t1 = at::randn({batch_size, hidden_size}, options);   auto t2 = at::randn({hidden_size}, options);   auto t3 = at::randn({hidden_size}, options);   auto t4 = at::randn({hidden_size}, options);    FusionExecutorCache fec(std::move(fusion_ptr));   auto cg_outputs = fec.runFusionWithInputs({t0, t1, t2, t3, t4});   testValidate(fusion, cg_outputs, {t0, t1, t2, t3, t4}, __LINE__, __FILE__); } Once we've fully developed Expr::evaluate for the majority of operators, we can start contemplating the retirement of cpp-repro-gen.py. In lieu of cpp-repro-gen.py, we should incorporate a method, Fusion::printCpp(), which will generate the necessary C++ code to recreate the fusion. The potential benefits of expanding Expr::evaluate are not confined to simplifying unit tests. It could also potentially improve how we schedule fusions. For instance, if we encounter a view or transpose on fusion inputs or outputs, we may choose not to include these operations in the kernel, but rather hoist them to ExpressionEvaluator. There's a specific aspect that warrants careful attention when developing Expr::evaluate: the ATen dependency. In the future, we may need to be able to build nvFuser without dependency on ATen. Therefore, it's preferable that we centralize any new code that depends on ATen. This way, we can easily guard these sections of code with macros in the future. Things to do Search for testValidate in our unit tests to identify which tests use testValidate. For each test, remove the ATen reference. Most likely, we'll encounter error messages about missing evaluate implementations. We should then provide the correct implementations for these missing evaluate methods. Preferably, we should keep PRs small, tackling only a few tests/operations in each PR. Once all the tests have been rectified, let's reassess the situation and determine whether it would be worth our time to remove cpp-repro-gen.py and implement Fusion::printCpp().

title: Race condition with "idling" branch overwriting shared memory in active branch. Failing test on Issue1133
author: jjsjann123
body: We start to see a failing test on issue 1133 since we updated our cuda toolkit. Turns out it's indeed a legit race issue with generated code. Where only the first few thread will be actively running reducing, while the rest are just idling. If we look at the generated code. We are using a shared memory T2[0] (line 32) to reduce each value before writing it to global memory T3. The race condition was reported between line 49 to line 58. So we have idling thread overwriting the reduction result before the "working" thread writes it to output. title: Serialization Benchmarking
author: rdspring1
body: This issue tracks which parts of the fusion cache hierarchy to prioritize during serialization. Comments:   Loading kernel database is non-trivial. Fixed via #814  Most of the time spent in GpuLower::lower is spent in IndexLowering::getIndexedExprs and ConditionalFromPredicateModifier. Prototype PR via #558  Scheduling the fusion and creating its Heuristics are slow.

title: Wrong unswitch predicate
author: naoyam
body: This fusion fails at the validation: TEST_F(NVFuserTest, Issue667Repro_CUDA) {   Fusion fusion;   FusionGuard fg(&fusion);    auto tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(2);   fusion.addInput(tv0);    auto tv1 = sum(tv0, {0, 1});   fusion.addOutput(tv1);    // [i0, i1]   tv1->split(1, 4);   // [i0, i1/4, 4]   tv1->merge(0);   // [i0*i1/4, 4]   tv1->split(0, 4);   // [i0*i1/4/4, 4, 4]   tv1->split(0, 1);   // [i0*i1/4/4, 1, 4, 4]    tv1->axis(1)->parallelize(ParallelType::Unswitch);    fusion.printKernel();    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   at::Tensor t0 = at::randn({4, 10}, options);   std::vector<c10::IValue> aten_inputs = {t0};    FusionExecutor fe;   fe.compileFusion(&fusion, aten_inputs);   auto outputs = fe.runFusion(aten_inputs);    auto ref = t0.to(at::kDouble).sum();    testValidate(       &fusion, outputs, aten_inputs, {ref}, __LINE__, __FILE__); }  I believe this is a simplified repro of the same issue as #667. The issue is the unswitch. If it's disabled, the validation passes. Here's the generated kernel. I disabled index hoisting and predicate elimination. __global__ void kernel1(Tensor<float, 2, 2> T0, Tensor<float, 0, 0> T1) {   NVFUSER_DEFINE_MAGIC_ZERO;   T1[0] = 0.00000000000000000e+00;   #pragma unroll 1   for(nvfuser_index_t i0 = 0; i0 < (ceilDiv((T0.logical_size[0] * (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4))), 4)); ++i0) {     if ((((3 + (4 * i0)) < (T0.logical_size[0] * (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4)))) && ((3 + (4 * ((3 + (4 * i0)) % (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4))))) < T0.logical_size[1]))) {       #pragma unroll       for(nvfuser_index_t i1 = 0; i1 < 4; ++i1) {         #pragma unroll         for(nvfuser_index_t i2 = 0; i2 < 4; ++i2) {           T1[0]             = T1[0]             + T0[((((((T0).alloc_stride)[0]) * (((4 * i0) + i1) / (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4)))) + ((4 * (((T0).alloc_stride)[1])) * (((4 * i0) + i1) % (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4))))) + ((((T0).alloc_stride)[1]) * (i2 + nvfuser_zero)))];         }       }       NVFUSER_UPDATE_MAGIC_ZERO;     } else {       #pragma unroll       for(nvfuser_index_t i1 = 0; i1 < 4; ++i1) {         #pragma unroll         for(nvfuser_index_t i2 = 0; i2 < 4; ++i2) {           if (((((4 * i0) + (i1 + nvfuser_zero)) < (T0.logical_size[0] * (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4)))) && (((4 * (((4 * i0) + i1) % (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4)))) + (i2 + nvfuser_zero)) < T0.logical_size[1]))) {             T1[0]               = T1[0]               + T0[((((((T0).alloc_stride)[0]) * (((4 * i0) + i1) / (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4)))) + ((4 * (((T0).alloc_stride)[1])) * (((4 * i0) + i1) % (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4))))) + ((((T0).alloc_stride)[1]) * (i2 + nvfuser_zero)))];           }         }       }       NVFUSER_UPDATE_MAGIC_ZERO;     }   } }  The problem is this predicate for the unswitch if statement: ((3 + (4 * ((3 + (4 * i0)) % (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4))))) < T0.logical_size[1])))   And in particular, this part: (3 + (4 * i0)) % (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4)). Suppose i0 == 0, the LHS of % is just 3. Since the RHS is also 3, this module result is just 0. However, when i1 is 2, this module is (2 + (4 * i0)) % (ceilDiv(T0.logical_size[1], 4)), so it's 2. So, for the i1 loop, we use 3 to generate the predicate for the end of the loop, but that's not the case generating the largest index due to the module operation. So, it seems that the assumption we have here (https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/csrc/device_lower/analysis/index_compute.cpp#L367) is not always valid.

title: Saving intermediate tensors between different fusion segments as fp16 may lead to inf values
author: liqiangxl
body: When layer norm backward is segmented, the intermediate tensors between different fusion segments are saved as fp16. In a case with a hidden size of 27K, it leads to inf values. To reproduce use: commit e3c9641 (HEAD -> llu/debug_fp16_overflow, origin/llu/debug_fp16_overflow) Validation error in output 0 on line 162 in file /opt/pytorch/nvfuser/test/test_combined_inner_outer_reduction.cpp.   Detected abs error of: inf  Debug shows the fp32 value (values in red box) is larger than the maximum fp16 value ( ~ 65504.) :  The error is due the cast to fp16 in the following consumer-produer chains.  If disable   castInputOutputToLowerPrecision(edges()); , case works fine. Are we supposed to do this cast? It is not safe and all the computations are done with fp32.

title: Remove `IrBuilder::newScalar` and `IrBuilder::newConstant`
author: zasdfgbnm
body: Due to historical reasons, IrBuilder::newScalar was added to create scalars. At that time, this makes sense, because a scalar can only be an int64_t, double, bool, or complex<double>, and we were using a separate class for each type. Therefore, it made sense to create a convenient helper function to dispatch based on the runtime type and create instances of these different classes. But today, this does not make sense any more: First, we now uses Val for scalars, and creating a scalar is as simple as IrBuilder::create<Val>(dtype) which does not have much more key strokes than IrBuilder::newScalar. On the other hand, scalars today can be an array, a struct, a pointer, and more crazy types. The name "scalar" no longer makes sense any more. Similarly, it no longer makes sense to have a IrBuilder::newConstant, because now the same functionality is as short as IrBuilder::create<Val>(val, dtype). I think we should just remove all IrBuilder::newScalar and IrBuilder::newConstant, and replace them with IrBuilder::create<Val>.

title: Setting `fusion_id_` with parallel threads may cause non-deterministic kernel names
author: naoyam
body: FusionExecutor::compileFusion may be executed in parallel by multiple threads, so incrementing fusion_id_ may result in data race. This can also lead to non-deterministic kernel numbers, which is inconvenient. Per @rdspring1, this could be avoided by passing fusion IDs to compileFusion.

title: Enable sync-free smem outer aliasing
author: jacobhinkle
body: Currently, allocations are re-used in two ways:  Aliasing, in which an allocation is re-used for another buffer without needing any thread synchronization Reallocation, in which synchronization causes no-longer-used tensor allocations to be re-used, allocating later tensors in their place.  Aliasing applies to both local memory and shared memory tensors, and reallocation only applies to shared memory tensors. The conditions for aliasing are quite strong, requiring the exact same size and index expressions for both allocations. Aliasing comes in two flavors: inner and outer. In inner aliasing, two tensors share the same inner loop, and their lifetimes within that scope do not overlap. If that is the case and their sizes and indices agree, and we are not resolving a broadcast which would result in repeated reads, then we can alias the tensors without any syncs, regardless of memory type. Outer aliasing is used in some cases where inner aliasing does not apply; inner aliasing is preferred in cases where both apply such as when the tensors are fully inlined. In outer aliasing, the two tensors do not share any loops, and their lifetimes at the outer scope do not overlap. In this case, for register/local tensors, it is safe to alias the tensors if their sizes match. This mode of aliasing is disallowed for shared memory tensors. Memory can still be reused if synchronizations exist, using reallocation. However, this should not always be required. If we had more sophisticated indexing analysis, we would be able to guarantee that each thread reads and writes a subset of elements from a shared memory allocation which does not overlap any subsets from other threads. See #739 (comment).

title: Outer live intervals should be closed intervals in aliasing pass
author: jacobhinkle

title: Change kernel naming scheme
author: rdspring1
body: Currently, the kernel name is defined as kernel + fusion_id_. (See https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/csrc/executor.h#L224-L228) This issue proposes that we use a more descriptive kernel name. kernel___[fusion_id_]___[pointwise, reduction, persistent, transpose, matmul scheduler type]___[gpu architecture] fusion_id_ requires tracking a static count of fusions in FusionExecutor class, which causes complications with parallel compilation (See Issue #762) and serialization. Here are some options to replace fusion_id_ in FusionExecutor.  Use the current number of fusions in FusionCache in python frontend. Hash timestamp with universal hash function.  // A simple universal hash function between [0, 21474836487] that shuffles numbers without collision. auto hash_fn = [a = 714468, b = 205029](int64_t x) {       auto linear_shift = a * x + b;       auto lower_half = linear_shift & 0xFFFF;       auto upper_half = linear_shift >> 16;       auto rotate = (lower_half << 16) | upper_half;       return rotate % 2147483648;     };

title: Run-to-run non-determinism in `TorchGatherSumAdd_CUDA` test
author: jacobhinkle
body: Running NVFUSER_DUMP=cuda_kernel nvfuser_tests --gtest_filter='*TorchGatherSumAdd*' multiple times gives different kernels currently on TOT (7aaa6c3). I have verified that the scheduler_params and fusion_ir printouts match, but the kernel_ir printout reflects the changes we see in the generated cuda code. The differences are typically like this:  Initially I thought this was because the inputs to the fusion, which are random, were not generated deterministically. However, I've verified that the random seeds are set properly and the inputs match. Additionally, different iterations of the test differ each time it is run. So I suspected there is nondeterminism in some lowering layer. Using lower_verbose, I think I've narrowed it down to replaceSymbolicSizes.

title: Consider not automatically reordering inner and outer domains
author: naoyam
body: Fuser/csrc/ir/nodes.cpp                   Lines 3355 to 3359       in       de03e5d                                                 if (axis_o > axis_i) {                                             auto tmp = axis_i;                                             axis_i = axis_o;                                             axis_o = tmp;                                           }                     TensorDomain::merge(int axis_o, int axis_i) automatically reorders axis_o and axis_i when axis_i is actually an outer position. This may be handy, but it also causes an ugly workaround when we really want to merge an inner domain and outer domain as outer and inner, respectively. See #767 (comment) I'm not sure if there's any code that relies on this automatic reordering. I myself didn't remember it. I'm feeling this reordering is not necessary but just unexpected and just honoring the order given as the function parameters seems to make more sense. CC: @jjsjann123, @zasdfgbnm

title: persistent scheduler refactor
author: liqiangxl
body: The persistent scheduler ScheduleHeuristic::Persistent evolves into a set of interconnected yet notably distinct strategies: innerPersistent, outerPersistent and  innerOuterPersistent. It is used to schedule fusions with both reductions and persistent buffers. Fusions with reduction that don't require persistent buffers are scheduled by ScheduleHeuristic::Reduction which is not a topic of this refactor although the method used here applies. The function checkCanSchedule utilizes both canScheduleCompileTime and canScheduleRunTime to determine the feasibility of scheduling a fusion. If deemed possible, the heuristic gets established by getPersistentHeuristics, leading to the fusion's scheduling via schedulePersistentKernel. Within these functions, they ascertain the type of reduction (inner, outer, or innerOuter) and apply various strategies based on the identified reduction type. Instead of cramming these diverse heuristics into one comprehensive scheduler, each could operate as an independent scheduler:  By doing this, the complexity of the persistent scheduler would be significantly reduced. A potential downside to this approach is the thrice-checking of the reduction type, specifically when the innerOuterPersistentScheduler proves to be the appropriate choice. Nonetheless, this can be sidestepped by harnessing specific cues from the fusion and directly dispatch to the appropriate scheduler instead of looping through every scheduler.

title: Unexpected behavior in `OptOutMutator`
author: jacobhinkle
body: Simple usage patterns of OptOutMutator give confusing behavior; I have run into these while exploring concretization of symbolic fusions. We should more clearly express any limitations on the expected usage of the class. Scope OptOutMutator is the only friend class of IrContainer and it is a friend to TensorView and so it's one of a handful of classes that can modify the TensorDomain of a tensor.  OptOutMutator is currently used as a parent class for  ValReplacementMutator : used by replaceValue ValReplacement::SubstituteInExpr : used by ir_utils::replaceValInExpr(Expr* expr, Val* reference, Val* substitute) which substitutes replaces the given expression if any of its inputs, outputs, or attributes is reference, replacing it with substitute. DynamicTransformConcretizer : used to concretize symbolic fusions by traversing and mutating TensorViews and their associated IterDomains.  Example of confusing behavior Here is the current docstring for OptOutMutator: // Class to perform mutations on Fusion IR. Exprs can simply be redefined, but // when mutating values they have to be registered through registerMutation so // that exprs can detect there's been a muatation and know to modify all // instances of that Val. This means each Val should be mutated "consistently". // Otherwise behavior may be difficult to understand as it depends on which // order mutate is called in. This class expects user to topologically call the // statments of interest so inputs are called and mutated before exprs depending // on them. // // Warning: TensorViews need to be treated carefully. As we don't generally // register their mutation when their tensor domains only change. If a TV needs // to be swapped out, it needs to be registered as a "proper" mutation like // other vals, on top of TensorDomain being updated in the mutated TensorView. Here is one use case from TensorView::cacheBefore where an output (this) of an expression is mutated using ir_utils::replaceValInExpr:   // Insert producer - Cache_Before (CB) - before this TV.   // Before: Prev TV -> [Definition Op] -> This TV   // After:  Prev TV -> [Definition Op] -> New CB TV -> [Set Op] -> This TV    // Get inputs for origin expression   auto expr_inputs = definition()->inputs();   // Expr* producer_definition =   ir_utils::replaceValInExpr(definition(), this, producer); This seems to work, since we use cacheBefore heavily and we do not see any errors. However, consider the following simple example: // Test that OptOutMutator mutates expressions in a predictable way TEST_F(NVFuserTest, OptOutMutatorMutatedOutput) {   std::unique_ptr<Fusion> fusion_ptr = std::make_unique<Fusion>();   Fusion* fusion = fusion_ptr.get();   FusionGuard fg(fusion);    TensorView* tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(1);   fusion->addInput(tv0);    auto tv1 = neg(tv0);    auto tv2 = set(tv1);   fusion->addOutput(tv2);    auto tv3 = set(tv0);    fusion->printMath(/*from_outputs_only*/ false); /* Inputs:   T0_g[ iS0{i0} ], float Outputs:   T2_g[ iS2{i0} ], float  %kernel_math { T1_l[ iS1{i0} ]    = -T0_g[ iS0{i0} ]; T2_g[ iS2{i0} ]    = Set( T1_l[ iS1{i0} ] ) T3_l[ iS3{i0} ]    = Set( T0_g[ iS0{i0} ] ) } */    OptOutMutator mut;   mut.registerMutation(tv1, tv3);   mut.mutate(tv1->definition());    fusion->printMath(/*from_outputs_only*/ false); /* Inputs:   T0_g[ iS0{i0} ], float Outputs:   T2_g[ iS2{i0} ], float  %kernel_math { T2_g[ iS2{i0} ]    = Set( T1_l[ iS1{i0} ] ) T3_l[ iS3{i0} ]    = -T0_g[ iS0{i0} ]; } */    auto options = at::TensorOptions().dtype(at::kFloat).device(at::kCUDA, 0);   at::Tensor t0 = at::randn({3}, options);    FusionExecutor fe;   fe.compileFusion(fusion); /* unknown file: Failure C++ exception with description "thread_predicates_.find(tv_inp) != thread_predicates_.end() INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/opt/pytor ch/nvfuser/csrc/device_lower/analysis/thread_predicate.cpp":255, please report a bug with repro script to NVFuser at https://gith ub.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/issues. Thread predicate map was not initialized, couldn't find T1_l[ iS5{( (( (( getMetaData(T0) )).logical_ size ))[0] )} ] Exception raised from updateBitSet at /opt/pytorch/nvfuser/csrc/device_lower/analysis/thread_predicate.cpp:255 (most recent call first): */    auto outputs = fe.runFusion({t0});    testValidate(fusion, outputs, {t0}, {t0}, __LINE__, __FILE__); } The neg op node was mutated, and its output tv1 had been registered for mutation to tv3. When that happened, the definition was transferred to tv3, which has the effect of redefining tv3 to the original definition of tv1! Compilation fails here; it seems that T1 is removed from the fusion, and we were perhaps just lucky to avoid a segfault when printing the second time. In any event I would have expected to see the following mutated fusion: Inputs:   T0_g[ iS0{i0} ], float Outputs:   T2_g[ iS2{i0} ], float  %kernel_math { T2_g[ iS2{i0} ]    = Set( T3_l[ iS3{i0} ] ) T3_l[ iS3{i0} ]    = Set( T0_g[ iS0{i0} ] ) }  Suggested approach I originally thought that we should just avoid mutating Exprs if only their outputs are registered for mutation, since this can have the effect of redefining the very Vals we had previously registered. However, the cacheBefore use case breaks in that case. We could salvage that by modifying cacheBefore to call replaceValInExpr on all uses of this instead. That is a typical pattern I use: replacing input and attribute vals in exprs, but not outputs. There may be other issues with this approach. I'm starting this issue to track this until we have a well-understood set of "guard rails" for mutating fusions.

title: Refactor: Move schedulers from registry.cpp to their own individual file
author: liqiangxl
body: The file registry.cpp is overloaded with content. It contains:  A namespace with utility functions for schedulers. A namespace that specifies all the schedulers along with their compile-time and runtime check methods. The SchedulerRuntimeInfo class. The SchedulerEntry class. The SchedulerEntryHash class. Debug printing methods for every heuristic.  Such structuring is not conducive to easy maintenance and future expansions. To improve its structure, we will:  Relocate each scheduler to its own individual .cpp file. Transfer the utility functions for schedulers to a dedicated utility file. Shift the debug printing methods for all heuristics to all_heuristics.cpp.  The goal is achieved by a serials of PRs. The first PR (#846 ) moves utility functions, persistent scheduler, and the debug printing methods as shown in the following figure  of steps (1) (2) (3) . Following PRs will finish steps (4) to (8).

title: Pad of Broadcast IterDomain broadcasts into the pad region
author: jacobhinkle
body: PR #841 enabled us to cat along broadcast IterDomains, by allowing those pads. In that case, the pad values are unused since they are predicated away. If we actually inspect the pad values, it seems they are incorrect: the broadcast value is being used in place of the pad value. See below: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from nvfuser import FusionDefinition, DataType  torch.manual_seed(0) inputs = [         torch.randn((1,), device='cuda'),         ]  with FusionDefinition() as fd:     x = fd.from_pytorch(inputs[0])     x_pad = fd.ops.pad(x, [1, 1])     fd.add_output(x_pad)  nvf_out = fd.execute(inputs) # With NVFUSER_DUMP=fusion_ir_preseg: # Inputs: #   T0_g[ bS0{1} ], float # Outputs: #   T1_g[ iS2{( ( ( (nvfuser_index_t)(1) ) + 1 ) + ( (nvfuser_index_t)(1) ) )}rf ], float #  # %kernel_math { # i6 = (nvfuser_index_t)(1); # i8 = (nvfuser_index_t)(1); # T1_g[ iS2{( ( ( (nvfuser_index_t)(1) ) + 1 ) + ( (nvfuser_index_t)(1) ) )}rf ] #    = pad( T0_g[ bS0{1} ], {i6, i8} ) # }  print(nvf_out[0]) # tensor([-0.9247, -0.9247, -0.9247], device='cuda:0') # Should be tensor([0, -0.9247, 0], device='cuda:0')  assert(torch.equal(nvf_out[0], F.pad(inputs[0], (1, 1)))) We see that the output IterType is Iteration, which rules out the possibility that the output was interpreted as an expanded broadcast instead of a pad. title: Redundant checks in getXheuristics and scheduleKernel
author: liqiangxl
body: getXheuristics (where X includes pointwise, persistent, reduction, transpose, matmul) is triggered within the heuristic constructor by computeHeuristics. The heuristic is already checked by the canScheduleCompileTime and canScheduleRunTime evaluations, ensuring that the fusion can be scheduled and executed. Consequently, additional checks in getXheuristics are redundant and should be removed. For example, in getTransposeHeuristics, the following check is reduandant as it is already done in canScheduleRunTime   NVF_ERROR(       !hasSmallTransposeDimensions(params) ||           scheduler_utils::getViewTVs(fusion).empty(),       "combination of view op with small transpose dimensions are not supported by transpose scheduler");  This check is also not trivial due to two nested loops in getViewTVs. Notably, in several cpp test cases, there's a direct utilization of getXheuristics. Developers should ensure the selecting of the appropriate heuristics. Alternatively, this API might need to be turned off in favor of exclusively using the ScheduleEntry API, as showcased in the softmax benchmark.   // Schedule through magic scheduler:   SchedulerRuntimeInfo runtime_info(fusion, aten_inputs);   NVF_ERROR(SchedulerEntry::canSchedule(       ScheduleHeuristic::Persistent, fusion, runtime_info));   auto scheduler = SchedulerEntry::makeEntry(       ScheduleHeuristic::Persistent, fusion, runtime_info);   scheduler->schedule(fusion);  Similar redundant checks exist for schedule function of some schedulers.

title: Reduce overhead in SchedulerEntry::proposeHeuristics
author: liqiangxl
body: SchedulerEntry::proposeHeuristics simply loops through the list of all the heuristics. Should have a better approach. The initial one can be: use ops defined in the fusion. The idea is to hoist some of the op checks from compileTimeCheck to proposeHeuristics. has_mma_op --> matmul, has_reduction_op --> further check persistent buffer -->   reduction or persistent

title: expand concretization to support opaque handling of stride order and shape specialization
author: jjsjann123
body: Proposal Add a concretization-like step to mutate TensorView definition with correct stride_order (allocationDomain) and contiguity flag. Context currently nvfuser API requires user to statically define broadcast dimensions as well as stride order (not even in our integration yet!) at the time when a fusion is defined. Any further update to the tensor shape / stride that contradicts these definition requires user/integration to handle that with a custom cache strategy. It is challenging to get a custom cache right, because of the complexity involved. The caching strategy in nvfuser evolves over time, which makes it even harder to maintain. We should try to keep this complexity inside nvfuser and abstract away such definition on user API. i.e. when we define a TensorView, we can specify only the rank of a tensor, without specifying the stride order or broadcast semantics. At runtime when a concrete input tensor is given, we can concretize the definition of each tensor, propagate that information to have a concrete fusion that can be scheduled. Eventually we would want to use this to handle both stirde_order as well as shape specialization (broadcast / size-0 or whatever new thing that pops up). TODO  We can take the initial step to support stride_order, since it's simpler to add and doesn't require propagation. It works very much like the reshape handling in concretization and is somewhat isolate from the rest of the cache system we have in our stack. The protocol for how to interpret a stride-order can be tricky and that propagation (if we want to do) is even harder. (for some fun context, look at these: pytorch/pytorch#23403 pytorch/pytorch#24090) But luckily once those are inside codegen logic, changing them would be relatively easy. So we don't have to make the right decision in the first place.

title: getXops in canScheduleCompileTime is overkill
author: liqiangxl
body: The canScheduleCompileTime function currently determines the existence of specific operations (such as reduction, matmul, SelectOp) by retrieving a vector of these operations and verifying if it's empty. This method can be streamlined. Instead of obtaining the entire vector, it's more efficient to simply check the presence of certain operations in the fusion. To address this, a two-step solution is proposed: (1) Refactor the existing getXops functions into a single templated function to centralize the operation retrieval logic. (2) Introduce a templated hasXops function, leveraging the refactored getXops, to directly check for the existence of specific operations without gathering them all.

title: Make matmul scheduler allocation-domain aware
author: zasdfgbnm
body: Currently, in scheduleMatmul, we are doing our analysis based on rFactor domain. For example, when there is a transpose, it will convert his transpose as a ldmatrix.trans. However, this behavior is not compatible with our long term design, which uses allocation domain to dictate allocation, and root/rfactor domain for semantics. So we should really be checking if there is a change in allocation, instead of checking the semantics. For example, if you have a PyTorch tensor A whose shape is [K, M] and whose stride is [1, K], and another PyTorch tensor B whose shape is [K, N] and stride [N, 1], and you do A.T @ B, then this should be treated as "no transposes" (MmaLayout::TT)

title: Add a new vectorization parallel type
author: zasdfgbnm
body: Currently, we supports two types of vectorization: Vectorize and MisalignedVectorize. Vectorize requires both the base address and the number of items to be a multiple of vector size. MisalignedVectorize requires neither of them to be a multiple of vectorize size, and does shifting on the fly. There can be another type of vectorization, which requires the base address to be a multiple of vector size, but not the number of items. Supporting this vectorization needs to leverage a feature in cp.async: https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/csrc/ops/arith.h  Instruction cp.async allows optionally specifying a 32-bit integer operand src-size. Operand src-size represents the size of the data in bytes to be copied from src to dst and must be less than cp-size. In such case, remaining bytes in destination dst are filled with zeros. Specifying src-size larger than cp-size results in undefined behavior.

title: We shouldn't require allocation domain to be between root and leaf
author: zasdfgbnm
body: Our current implementation for swizzle is very hacky and broken: #554 Assume that we have a fusion Tswizzled = T0 T1 = Tswizzled  the indexing we want for swizzle is like this Tswizzled[swizzled_index] = T0[index] T1[index] = Tswizzled[swizzled_index]  The most natural way to implement this behavior is by making allocation domain not required to be between root and leaf. Instead, for Tswizzled, we can have: allocation domain: [I1, I2] I3, I4 = swizzle2d(I1, I2) root domain: [I3, I4] ... transformations ... leaf domain: [..., BIDx, TIDx, Vec]  Then when indexing Tswizzled as consumer, we are already indexing into allocation domain, we will automatically get the swizzled index. When indexing Tswizzled as producer, we first replay Tswizzled as T1, which is trivial in this case. We do not need any hacks like "skipSwizzles" to support this.

title: Enhancing InnerOuterPersistent Scheduler for unmatched iter-reduction domains.
author: liqiangxl
body: Current InnerOuterPersistent scheduler requires all the iteration domains of the inner reduction tv are mapped to reduction domains of the outer reduction tv. For example: Inputs:   T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2}, iS2{i3} ], float Outputs:   T3_g[ iS9{i0}, iS10{i2}, iS11{i3} ], float   T4_g[ rS12{i0}, iS13{i2}, iS14{i3} ], float  %kernel_math { T1_l[ iS3{i0}, iS4{i2}, rS5{i3} ]    = reduction( T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2}, iS2{i3} ], op = add, initial value = float(0), allreduce = false ) T2_l[ iS6{i0}, iS7{i2}, bS8{1} ]    = broadcast( T1_l[ iS3{i0}, iS4{i2}, rS5{i3} ] ) T3_g[ iS9{i0}, iS10{i2}, iS11{i3} ]    = T2_l[ iS6{i0}, iS7{i2}, bS8{1} ]    + T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2}, iS2{i3} ]; T4_g[ rS12{i0}, iS13{i2}, iS14{i3} ]    = reduction( T0_g[ iS0{i0}, iS1{i2}, iS2{i3} ], op = add, initial value = float(0), allreduce = false )   In this fusion, inner reduction is T1_g[ iS3{i0}, iS4{i2}, rS5{i3} ], outer reduction is T4_g[ rS12{i0}, iS13{i2}, iS14{i3} ], The axis iS4{i2} in T1_g should be a reduction in T4_g, otherwise we can't do a partial outer reduction while iterating the iteration domain of inner reduction. See test case CombinedSchedulerInnerOuterMismatch and issue #1023

title: thread block cluster reduction using distributed shared memory
author: liqiangxl
body: Goal: Implement thread block cluster parallelism and cluster reduction using distributed shared memory. Steps: (1) Add thread block cluster parallelism and initiate the kernel with the defined cluster dimensions. (2) Add cluster reduction using distributed shared memory spanning multiple thread blocks. (3) Determine conditions under which cluster reduction should supplant grid reduction.

title: un-aligned warp reduction
author: liqiangxl
body: current codegen allows un-aligned warp reduction, which is not safe since the assuption of the implementation is all the threads in the same warp are participating. To illustrate this, a repo with a test case named TEST_F(NVFuserTest, UnAlignedWarpReduce) has been added. This test conducts a warp reduction on 17 elements using 17 threads, while the remaining 15 threads in the same warp execute the warp::warpReduceTIDX from the else branch. Although it is unsafe (the behavior of threads not participating is un-defined), the test can still pass, at least in my local node. Generated code: __global__ void kernel1(Tensor<float, 2, 2> T0, Tensor<float, 1, 1> T3) {   alignas(16) extern __shared__ char array[];   void* shared_mem = array;   nvfuser_index_t i0;   i0 = T0.alloc_stride[1LL] * ((nvfuser_index_t)threadIdx.x);   bool b1;   b1 = ((nvfuser_index_t)threadIdx.x) < T0.logical_size[1LL];   bool b2;   b2 = ((nvfuser_index_t)threadIdx.x) == 0LL;   if (b1) {     #pragma unroll 1     for(nvfuser_index_t i3 = 0LL; i3 < T0.logical_size[0LL]; ++i3) {       float T2[1LL];       T2[0LL] = 0.000000000e+00f;       float T1[1LL];       T1[0LL] = 0.000000000e+00f;       T1[0LL]         = T0[(i0 + (T0.alloc_stride[0LL] * i3))]         + (float) 1.00000000000000000e+00;       warp::warpReduceTIDX<true, false>(T2[0LL], T1[0LL], [](float &a, float b) { a = a + b; }, static_cast<float*>(shared_mem), true, static_cast<float>(0.000000000e+00f));       if (b2) {         T3[i3]           = T2[0LL]           + (float) 1.00000000000000000e+00;       }     }   } else {     #pragma unroll 1     for(nvfuser_index_t i3 = 0LL; i3 < T0.logical_size[0LL]; ++i3) {       float T2[1LL];       T2[0LL] = 0.000000000e+00f;       float T1[1LL];       T1[0LL] = 0.000000000e+00f;       if (b1) {         T1[0LL]           = T0[(i0 + (T0.alloc_stride[0LL] * i3))]           + (float) 1.00000000000000000e+00;       }       warp::warpReduceTIDX<true, false>(T2[0LL], T1[0LL], [](float &a, float b) { a = a + b; }, static_cast<float*>(shared_mem), true, static_cast<float>(0.000000000e+00f));       if (b2) {         T3[i3]           = T2[0LL]           + (float) 1.00000000000000000e+00;       }     }   }  Added printf to mark two different diverged calls of warp::warpReduceTIDX. title: Avoid `#pragma unroll` in split-K reduction loop
author: jacobhinkle
body: @mmigdal-nv and I came across this when benchmarking #1002. We noticed that with splitk_factor=1 the compile times were about 1-2 seconds, but with splitk_factor>1 they were >20 s. The register usage in this case goes from 238 to 250, which is close to the max of 255. @mmigdal-nv also noticed that the PTX file goes from about 50KB to >500KB and speculated that these effects may be due to unrolling the loop containing the gridReduce. That loop looks like this:   #pragma unroll   for(nvfuser_index_t i116 = 0; i116 < 4; ++i116) {     nvfuser_index_t i117;     i117 = 32 * i116;     nvfuser_index_t i118;     i118 = i44 + (i45 * i116);     nvfuser_index_t i119;     i119 = -(16LL * i116);     #pragma unroll     for(nvfuser_index_t i120 = 0; i120 < 4; ++i120) {       nvfuser_index_t i121;       i121 = i117 + (4 * i120);       nvfuser_index_t i122;       i122 = 16LL * i120;       nvfuser_index_t i123;       i123 = i118 + i122;       nvfuser_index_t i124;       i124 = -i122;       #pragma unroll       for(nvfuser_index_t i125 = 0; i125 < 2; ++i125) {         nvfuser_index_t i126;         i126 = i121 + (2LL * i125);         nvfuser_index_t i127;         i127 = 8LL * i125;         nvfuser_index_t i128;         i128 = i123 + i127;         bool b129;         b129 = i56 < (i124 - i127);         bool b130;        b130 = b58 && b129;         #pragma unroll         for(nvfuser_index_t i131 = 0; i131 < 2; ++i131) {           nvfuser_index_t i132;           i132 = i126 + (16 * i131);           bool b133;           b133 = i57 < (i119 - (8LL * i131));           bool b134;           b134 = b129 && b133;           Array<float, 2, 2> T5;           #pragma unroll           for(nvfuser_index_t i135 = 0; i135 < 2; ++i135) {             T5[i135] = 0.00000000000000000e+00;           }           #pragma unroll           for(nvfuser_index_t i135 = 0; i135 < 2; ++i135) {             reduction::gridReduce<false, false, true, false, false, false, false, true>(               T5[i135],               T10[(i132 + i135)],               [](float &a, float b) { a = a + b; },               &T11[0],               &T12[0],               static_cast<float*>(shared_mem),               b134,               b134,               float(0.00000000000000000e+00),               ((((((((i116 * (ceilDiv(64, 16))) + i120) * (ceilDiv(16, 8))) + i125) * (ceilDiv(16, 8))) + i131) * 2LL) + i135),               (((((ceilDiv(64, 16)) * (ceilDiv(64, 16))) * (ceilDiv(16, 8))) * (ceilDiv(16, 8))) * 2LL));           }           if ((b130 && b133)) {             loadLocalToGlobal<float, /*vec_size=*/2, /*is_volatile=*/false>( &T4[(i128 + (i46 * i131))], &T5[0]);           }         }       }     }   } Just removing the #pragma unroll on the entire loop nest shown here reduces registers from 250 to 248, reduces ptx file size back to around 75KB, and reduces the compile time back to 1-2s, but at the expense of introducing a 512B stack. The resulting kernel runs roughly as fast or maybe slightly faster as well. This might mean we need to do some more sophisticated analysis here: https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/blob/main/csrc/index_compute.cpp#L1447-L1454.

title: low performance for kernel with padded dim and RNG Ops
author: liqiangxl
body: In this case, bdimx is padded from 106 to 128 and the prediate in else branch for RNG Ops is removed. This lead to performance regression compared with unpadded version as discussed in #988. Performance data for different tests:    Test latency, ms     padded (main branch) 0.74   unpadded 0.56   padded with predicate 0.58   unpadded with predicate 0.56    To solve this issue, we can: (1) don't eliminate predicate for RNG Ops (2) use unpadded kernel. math.sqrt(embed_dim_per_head)      # batch size, head count, sequence length, sequence length     T0 = fd.define_tensor(shape=[-1, -1, -1, -1], contiguity=[True, True, True, True], dtype=input_dtype, is_cpu=False)     T1 = fd.define_tensor(shape=[-1, -1], contiguity=[True, True], dtype=input_dtype, is_cpu=False)     if input_dtype == DataType.Half:         T0 = fd.ops.cast(T0, title: segmentation due to insufficient register size in `innerOuterPersistentHeuristic`
author: liqiangxl
body: Background: The innerOuterPersistentHeuristic needs additional persistent tensors to store the intermediate outer reduction results apart from the original cached input tensors. The summary below outlines the number of persistent tensors requested and the maximum element count that can be processed assuming all 64K registers are used to store persistent buffers:    Model Intermediate Tensor CachedInput Tensor Buffer Size Per Element max elements if given 64K registers     LayerNormBwd 2 fp32 3 fp16/32 14 (fp16), 20 (fp32) 18.3K (fp16), 12.8K (fp32)   RMSNormBwd 1 fp32 3 fp6/33 10 (fp16), 16 (fp32) 25.6K (fp16), 16K (fp32)    In the current scheduler, the number of available registers has been adjusted to prevent segmentation for cases with large hidden sizes. For instance, with fp32, up to 70K registers are permissible. Yet, any further increment in the permitted register count can lead to significant register spills, resulting in performance regression. With segmentation, there's typically a 40% to 50% performance reduction. To bypass segmentation, potential solutions include:  use both smem and register for persistent buffer. Thread Block Cluster Reduction: This is a feature present in H100. Cross Grid Reduction.  Design for Approach-1: Utilizing both Shared Memory (smem) and Registers for Persistent Buffer The fundamental algorithm will be anchored in the getPersistentBufferStorageParams function. This function will return a structure containing information about which tensor views (tv) should be transferred to shared memory, as well as the buffer sizes for shared memory and registers. It will also detail if the device has adequate registers and shared memory and if the buffers should be projected to inputs. Structure Definition struct PersistentBufferStorageParams {   std::vector<TensorView*> smem_persistent_tvs; // Tensor views to be transferred to shared memory   int64_t smem_buffer_size = -1;   int64_t regs_buffer_size = -1;   int64_t smem_overhead = -1;   bool has_enough_regs_and_smem = false;   bool project_to_input = false; };  Buffer Size Calculation & Insufficient Register Handling Should the registers be inadequate for holding the persistent buffers, the following procedure is executed: (1) Candidate Sorting: Populate sorted_candidate_tvs with candidate tensor views in a priority sequence determined by the sort_buffer_tvs() function. The sorting criteria aim to reduce both global memory to shared memory (gmem->smem) and shared memory to register (smem->register) data transfers. The sorting encompasses three priority levels:    Priority level Item justification     1 prioritize tvs with small data type sizes minimize both gmem->smem and smem/register traffic   2 prioritize tvs used in outer broadcast minimize gmem->smem traffic. These tvs are reused in every grid loop.   3 prioritize tvs with less consumers minimize smem->register traffic.    (2) Buffer Size Accumulation: Compute the cumulative buffer size by aggregating across sorted_candidate_tvs. For instance, acc_regs_buffer_sizes[i] represents the cumulative buffer size of the first i buffers according to their sequence in sorted_candidate_tvs. (3) Shared Memory Allocation:  Identify the minimum number of tensor views that need to be transferred to comply with size constraints. Log these tensor views Mark them for shared memory storage in the schedulePersistentKernel function.

title: Plumb automatic schedulers into Python interface
author: jacobhinkle
body: For autotuning, and for developing heuristics, it would be convenient to be able to schedule complicated fusions from the Python side. Currently, doing so requires us to write the whole schedule from the primitives like split, parallelize, etc. However, it would be great to be able to create in Python some surrogate of, say a PointwiseParams or MatmulParams object and call schedulePointwise or scheduleMatmul with it. The key is that this would let us manipulate the heuristic in order to explore different regimes of our automatic schedulers, without needing to reproduce the complicated logic in the schedule* functions. Each param object inherits from HeuristicParams but appends a number of custom attributes, some of which are compound types. For example, MatmulParams contains, among other things, a MatMulTileOptions struct that contains multiple GemmTile structs each holding a triple of ints. We could represent this with a dict in Python, but we will need to maintain a translation function for each type heuristic parameter object. Instead we could try to devise a system where we could automatically convert from a nested dictionary of simple types. For example, each of the structs would declare names and types for their members using a macro that would generate the conversion code. struct GemmTile : public FromDict {  FROM_DICT_INT_ATTR(m);  FROM_DICT_INT_ATTR(n);  FROM_DICT_INT_ATTR(k);   // rest of definition unmodified  }  struct MatMulTileOptions : public FromDict {   FROM_DICT_CLASS_ATTR(GemmTile, cta_tile, 128, 128, 32);   FROM_DICT_CLASS_ATTR(GemmTile, warp_tile, 64, 64, 32);   FROM_DICT_CLASS_ATTR(GemmTile, instruction_tile, 16, 8, 16);   // ... }  // HeuristicParams would inherit from FromDict struct MatmulParams : public HeuristicParams {   // ...   FROM_DICT_BOOL_ATTR(async_gmem_load_operands, false);   FROM_DICT_CLASS_ATTR(MatMulTileOptions, tile_sizes);   // ... }  // Then we'd automatically generate a static method // MatmulParams MatmulParams::fromDict(const std::unordered_map<std::string, std::variant<...>>& d); Plumbing these in to the python frontend would then be very simple, and presumably this would also make serde simple for the heuristic info. Is it possible to create such a class FromDict and associated macros? Is this pattern already implemented somewhere?

title: Evaluate using Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO) and LLVM BOLT
author: zamazan4ik
body: Hi! Recently I checked Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO) improvements on multiple projects. The results are here. E.g. PGO results for LLVM-related tooling are here. According to the tests, PGO usually helps with the compiler and compiler-like workloads (like static analysis) - e.g. Clang gets +20% compilation speed with PGO. I think trying to optimize the Fuser compiler with PGO can be a good way to reduce Fuser's CPU usage. I can suggest the following action points:  Perform PGO benchmarks on Fuser. If it shows improvements - add a note to the documentation about improvements in Fuser's compiler performance with PGO. Providing an easier way (e.g. a build option) to build scripts with PGO can be helpful for the end-users and maintainers since they will be able to optimize the Fuser compiler according to their own workloads. Optimize pre-built Fuser binaries.  Testing Post-Link Optimization techniques (like LLVM BOLT) would be interesting too (Clang and Rustc already use BOLT as an addition to PGO) but I recommend starting from the usual PGO. Here are some examples of how PGO optimization is integrated in other projects:  Rustc: a CI script for the multi-stage build GCC:  Official docs, section "Building with profile feedback" (even AutoFDO build is supported) A part in a "wonderful" configure script   Clang: Docs Python:  CPython: README Pyston: README   Go: Bash script V8: Bazel flag ChakraCore: Scripts Chromium: Script Firefox: Docs  Thunderbird has PGO support too   PHP - Makefile command and old Centminmod scripts MySQL: CMake script YugabyteDB: GitHub commit FoundationDB: Script Zstd: Makefile Foot: Scripts Windows Terminal: GitHub PR Pydantic-core: GitHub PR file.d: GitHub PR OceanBase: CMake flag NodeJS: Configure script

title: Clear the ambiguity for allocation domain when contiguity isn't required.
author: jjsjann123
body: alloc_domain is accompanied by contiguity flags. For entries where the correponding contiguity flags is marked as true, the semantics for alloc_domain is well defined. i.e. The stride on the outer dimension needs to be equal to the product of the size and stride on its inner neighboring dimension. Given a simple example, where alloc_dom is identical to root_dom. TV0: root_dom: i0, i1, i2 alloc_dom: i0, i1, i2 contiguity: F, T, F With the contiguity flag, the only "rigid" requirement (Because tv->contiguity[1] == true) is that tv0->stride(1) == tv->size(2) * tv->stride(2). The question here is, what does the order in alloc_dom mean in this scenario? Should we stick to the assumption that alloc_dom order here dictates that tv0->stride(0) >= tv0->stride(1) >= tv0->stride(2)? Functional-wise, it's safe to relax the check here and not enforce the order of strides, which allows us more kernel re-use -> in implementation, we need to refactor how we compute cache/descriptor on tensor to support that. Meanwhile, in theory our scheduler might be relying on the stride-order for efficient scheduling. However, how much does that matter in reality for dimensions that's not collapsible and isn't contiguous in memory remains a quesion. Note: The original question showed up in this conversation: #1167 (comment)

title: Slow compile times with single-kernel split-K
author: jacobhinkle
body: The current version of single-kernel split-K introduced in #1002 calls gridReduce in an innermost loop that, when unrolled, replicates that large inlined function 128 times. This causes a drastic slowdown in the NVRTC compilation time (from <1 second to >20 seconds). Adding __noinline__ to the gridReduce declaration returns the compile time to normal, at the expense of introducing a small stack frame due to the function call. This might be acceptable in the split-K case since the call is repeated so many times and the stack is likely to stay within L1, but it might negatively impact performance in other reduction use cases. Related to #991.

title: Split-K matmul is slow even for few partitions
author: jacobhinkle
body: Our current split-K kernels are quite slow. For example, these are the two split-K problems I encountered with a bfloat16 fwd+bwd nanogpt run (both are TST, NN, no epilogue), measured on an A100:   Note that M and N match between these cases: the only difference is K, which is much larger in the first plot. Larger K shows that quantization has a large effect on runtime in the first case, which for the smaller problem, the reduction needed for our split-K seems to drastically increase runtime. Cublas uses a single kernel with in-place reduction in this case, and in most of the important GEMMs I've observed in real networks so far (please reply with an example if there are important two-kernel GEMMs I missed). Possible approach: grouped reduction In the case of allreduce and welford+broadcast, we have the ability to do a "cross-iteration grouped reduction". This is a notion that is related to but distinct from "horizontally grouped reduction", which refers to executing multiple reduction operations simultaneously (e.g. a sum and a max)  which enables sharing synchronization. Instead, cross-iteration grouping refers to the use of ParallelType::Group to indicate some unparallelized non-reduction axes in a single reduction which should be converted to tuple and reduced as one unit. This enables us to reduce the amount of synching required by a factor equal to the number of elements in the grouped loop nest. For example, consider this pseudo-code which is doing 8 separate reductions: #pragma unroll for (auto i1: irange(2)) {   #pragma unroll   for (auto i2: irange(4)) {     out[i1*4+ i2] = gridReduce(in[i1* 4 + i2], [](float a, float b) { return a+b; });   } } Each grid reduction will perform a separate block and grid sync, and each element will be reduced separately. Incidentally, placing this heavy inline function inside an unrolled loop nest slows down compilation a lot (#1242). Instead, grouping the i1 and i2 axes results in something like groupedGridReduce(  // actually uses reduction::ParallelReduce   /*out*/makeTuple<       out[0], out[1], out[2], out[3],       out[4 + 0], out[4 + 1], out[4 + 2], out[4 + 3]>,   /*in*/makeTuple<       in[0], in[1], in[2], in[3],       in[4 + 0], in[4 + 1], in[4 + 2], in[4 + 3]>,    [](float a, float b) { return a+b; } ); However, this is currently implemented with a type-level tuple and only supports grouping sizes of 1 thru 8, or 16. Most of our matmul kernels have 128 reductions to group, which will be cumbersome to support in the tuple approach. Eliminating the workspace Reducing the amount of synchronization means that we typically would need to use a larger workspace. To see this, consider that our current approach is such that only a single element in each reduction segment is reduced at once, so we only need a global workspace buffer whose size is num_segments*blocks_per_segment. Synchronizing at the outer loop level means we would need num_segments*blocks_per_segment*reductions_per_segment to avoid data hazards. The factor blocks_per_segment comes from our current approach where we asynchronously write from every block and then the last block in each segment waits to perform the final sum. Instead, we can serialize the blocks so that each block watches a semaphore for its turn to read and write its individual work buffer element. That reduces the required workspace to num_segments * reductions_per_segment which is equal to the total number of reductions being performed; in the case of a matmul, this is the size of the output tensor. We can then enable our aliasing analysis to re-use the output buffer for this purpose instead of creating a new intermediate tensor. ### Tasks - [ ] https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/pull/1405 - [ ] https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/pull/1456 - [ ] https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/pull/1510 - [ ] https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/pull/1528 - [ ] https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/pull/1534 - [ ] ~~Enable inner aliasing of global buffers~~

title: Possible performance opportunities for fused matmul kernels
author: drzejan2
body: Issue summary: For matmul fusions with more than single output (epilogue with aux tensor) in some fusions the processing of the output tensors is performed in two identical loops that could be merged. The performance gain could be achieved by reducing the number of access to shared memory by each thread. Reproduction: The code has been generated for MatmulSchedulerTest/PrecisionParametrizedTest.EpilogueReluAux/HSH test case on A100 GPU. The test has been added in #1191 and enabled in #1314. The generated epilogue code looks like this: // NOTE: move matmul result data from register to shared memory, with unswizzling #pragma unroll for(nvfuser_index_t i115 = 0; i115 < 4; ++i115) {   nvfuser_index_t i116 = 16 * i115;   nvfuser_index_t i117 = i46 + (512LL * i115);   #pragma unroll   for(nvfuser_index_t i118 = 0; i118 < 4; ++i118) {     nvfuser_index_t i119 = i116 + (4 * i118);     nvfuser_index_t i120 = i12 + i118;     nvfuser_index_t i121 = (i117 + (32LL * (i120 / 4))) + (8LL * (i47 ^ (i120 % 4)));     #pragma unroll     for(nvfuser_index_t i122 = 0; i122 < 2; ++i122) {       loadGeneric<float, 2>( &T11[(i121 + (256LL * i122))],  &T5[(i119 + (2LL * i122))]);     }   } } __syncthreads();  // NOTE: stores matmul output after down casting to fp16 #pragma unroll for(nvfuser_index_t i123 = 0; i123 < 8; ++i123) {   nvfuser_index_t i124 = i48 + (1024 * i123);   Array<__half, 8, 8> T9;   #pragma unroll   for(nvfuser_index_t i125 = 0; i125 < 8; ++i125) {     nvfuser_index_t i126 = i49 + i125;     nvfuser_index_t i127 = i126 / 32;     nvfuser_index_t i128 = i126 % 32;     nvfuser_index_t i129 = i128 / 8;     T9[i125] = __float2half(T11[((((i124 + (32LL * i127)) + (32LL * (i129 / 4))) + (8LL * ((i127 % 4) ^ (i129 % 4)))) + (i128 % 8))]);   }   if ((b53 && (i58 < (-(32 * i123))))) {     loadLocalToGlobal<__half, /*vec_size=*/8, /*is_volatile=*/false>( &T6[(i51 + (i52 * i123))], &T9[0]);   } }  // NOTE: applies relu on matmul output and downcast it to fp16 #pragma unroll for(nvfuser_index_t i130 = 0; i130 < 8; ++i130) {   nvfuser_index_t i131 = i48 + (1024 * i130);   Array<__half, 8, 8> T10;   #pragma unroll   for(nvfuser_index_t i132 = 0; i132 < 8; ++i132) {     nvfuser_index_t i133 = i49 + i132;     nvfuser_index_t i134 = i133 / 32;     nvfuser_index_t i135 = i133 % 32;     nvfuser_index_t i136 = i135 / 8;     float T7[1];     T7[0] = relu(T11[((((i131 + (32LL * i134)) + (32LL * (i136 / 4))) + (8LL * ((i134 % 4) ^ (i136 % 4)))) + (i135 % 8))]);     T10[i132] = __float2half(T7[0]);   }   if ((b53 && (i58 < (-(32 * i130))))) {     loadLocalToGlobal<__half, /*vec_size=*/8, /*is_volatile=*/false>( &T8[(i51 + (i52 * i130))], &T10[0]);   } }  Other details:  original discussion about the generated code: link code generated for A100 device build / test environment  docker image: pjnl-latest, docker sha: 7e6b123c8f2411eefc7bb15d0b7294e2c8e89a7a16e1a0db6db10b47c6872636

title: Over estimation of persistent buffer size when project persistent buffer to its persistent producers
author: liqiangxl
body: In normalization scheduler, if project_persistent_buffers = True, PersistentBufferProjector will project persistent tvs to inputs, otherwise it trys to project persistent tvs to its immediate persistent producers. See #419 and #343 However, the buffer size was over estimated in scheduler_utils::persistentBufferSize. This overestimation occurs because the potential to project persistent tvs onto their immediate persistent producers isn't factored into the calculations. For example, in the following fusion, T7 and T11 are persistent, both of them can be projected to inputs. The current calculated persistent_buffer_size is based on the reduction dim of T7 and T11. The projected_persistent_buffer_size  is based on the correponding dim of inputs T0, T1, and T2.  If the inputs are fp16, the projected_persistent_buffer_size is smaller than persistent_buffer_size and project_persistent_buffers = True. However, since T11 can be projected back to T7, the correct value of persistent_buffer_size  should only include the reduction dim of T7. Then, the projected_persistent_buffer_size is larger than persistent_buffer_size and the correct value of project_persistent_buffers should be False.

title: symbolic iterdomain needs special handling on broadcast check.
author: jjsjann123
body: Our new reshape API introduces symbolic iterdomain, which leaves isBroadcast() on symbolic iterdomain non-determined until concretization. There's issue #1393, which our c++ expand API asserts when we try to expand a symbolic iterdomain, even though it has a static extent 1. @jacobhinkle gave a more general example than the one in the original issue here: #1394 (comment)   auto tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(2);   fusion->addInput(tv0);    auto s0 = IrBuilder::create<Val>(DataType::Index);   auto s1 = IrBuilder::create<Val>(DataType::Index);   auto s2 = IrBuilder::create<Val>(DataType::Index);   fusion->addInput(s0);   fusion->addInput(s1);   fusion->addInput(s2);   fusion->addInput(s3);    auto tv1 = reshape(tv0, {s0, s1});   auto tv2 = expand(tv1, {s0, s2});    fusion->addOutput(tv2);  Since the reshape here is symbolic and dynamic, we can only determine the semantic after concretization. So two things needs to be done:  c++ API needs to relax the check on isBroadcast() for operations like expand / squeeze e.t.c.. We can probably have a new maybeBroadcast() on TensorView/TensorDomain. we also needs to add a checkConcretization as suggested #1394 (comment)

title: trivial AllocDomain causes performance regression
author: jjsjann123
body: I noticed that when we pass in fusion with all inputs marked with explicit alloc_domain, even though it's identical to rfactor_domain, there was a performance regression. title: Alias analysis between outputs.
author: jjsjann123
body: Currently our alias analysis only handles output to input / output to output. This is slightly different from what bookend optimization does, which seems to give better perf in some attention block. Bookend optimization would strip meta-operation (view/squeeze/slice e.t.c.) on the bookend of a fusion and pass in tensor with mutated strides. This should be doable given the alias analysis information. We just need some mechanics to plumb this through our segmenter to know when and where to stop merging segments, as well as when to initiate segmentation even though the entire fusion could be scheduled as a single kernel. For example, when we handle meta operations on inputs, we might need to consider whether stripping aliases are beneficial, even though they give a slightly smaller fusion IR.   auto tv0 = makeSymbolicTensor(2);   auto s0 = IrBuilder::create<Val>(DataType::Index);   auto s1 = IrBuilder::create<Val>(DataType::Index);   auto tv1 = unsqueeze(tv0, -1);   auto tv2 = expand(tv1, {s0, s1});   // ... some fusion uses both tv0 and tv2  If we decided to strip the unsqueeze and expand from the actual codegen kernel, we are going to pass two tensor inputs to the kernel tv0 and tv2 here. Even though the two tensors are just aliasing and cache would help us, it might still be worth keeping these operations just so we have a single input to the fusion.

title: Failed chain projections when project persistent buffer to its persistent producers
author: liqiangxl
body: In normalization scheduler, persistent tvs can be projected to its immediate persistent producers if project_persistent_buffers = False. However, current implentation fails if a chain projection is required. Consider the following case where T1, T2, T3 are persistent buffers, ideally, T2 and T3 should be projected to T1.       T1 = f(T0); Tx = add(T1, broadcast(sum(T1)));       T2 = f(T1); Ty = add(T2, broadcast(sum(T2)));       T3 = f(T2); Tz = add(T3, broadcast(sum(T3)));  If T2 is projected to T1 before T3 is projected, we get:       T1 = f(T0); Tx = add(T1, broadcast(sum(T1)));       T2 = f(T1); Ty = add(f(T1), broadcast(sum(T2)));       T3 = f(f(T1)); Tz = add(T3, broadcast(sum(T3)));  Then, T3's producer is changed to f(T1) which is not a persistent tensor. So T3 can't be projected back to T1. To fix this issue, we should: set a projection order based on dependencies. In this case, the visiting order should be [T3, T2, T1]. After project T3 to its producers, we have:  Tz = add(f(T2),broadcast(sum(T3)));  Then,  continue project T2 to its producers, we have:       Tz = add(f(f(T1)),broadcast(sum(T3)));       Ty = add(f(T1), broadcast(sum(T2)));  The only left persistent buffer is T1.

title: OOM error
author: naoyam
body: There's a persisting OOM error recently. See for example https://github.com/NVIDIA/Fuser/actions/runs/7032815711, which was a CI test for PR #1319. The specific test failing is GpuViewTest.FusionReshapeVectorize. There was an attempt to fix the error (#1382), but apparently it was not enough. The error message seems to suggest there's something occupying a large chunk of GPU memory aside from the PyTorch itself: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 256.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 15.78 GiB of which 20.75 MiB is free. Process 3304 has 15.76 GiB memory in use. Of the allocated memory 8.76 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, and 55.88 MiB is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated. If reserved but unallocated memory is large try setting PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True to avoid fragmentation. See documentation for Memory Management (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html#environment-variables)  Here, PyTorch itself only used 8.75 GB, but the total usage was 15.76 GB, and we don't know where the remaining 7 GB went.

title: Stop generating code for alias outputs.
author: wujingyue
body: Currently, we do that for fusions of which all outputs are aliases. However, even when some but not all outputs are aliases, we can skip generating lots of code. This is a real use case found in GPT2: def nvfuser_fusion_id20(fd : FusionDefinition) -> None :     T0 = fd.define_tensor(shape=[-1, -1, -1], contiguity=[True, True, True], dtype=DataType.BFloat16, is_cpu=False)     S1 = fd.define_scalar(2048, dtype=DataType.Int)     S2 = fd.define_scalar(2304, dtype=DataType.Int)     V3 = fd.define_vector([S1, S2], dtype=DataType.Int)     T4 = fd.ops.reshape(T0, new_shape=V3)     T5 = fd.ops.permute(T4, dims=[1, 0])     T6 = fd.ops.cast(T0, dtype=DataType.Float)     T7 = fd.ops.sum(T6, axes=[0, 1], keepdim=False, dtype=DataType.Null)     T8 = fd.ops.cast(T7, dtype=DataType.BFloat16)     S9 = fd.define_scalar(2048, dtype=DataType.Int)     S10 = fd.define_scalar(2304, dtype=DataType.Int)     V11 = fd.define_vector([S9, S10], dtype=DataType.Int)     T12 = fd.ops.reshape(T0, new_shape=V11)     fd.add_output(T12)     fd.add_output(T5)     fd.add_output(T8)  T12 and T5 are aliases of T0, and T8 is not.

title: Break up the C++ test executable
author: naoyam
body: Currently, one executable, nvfuser_tests, contains all the C++ tests. It seems we are beginning to see the impact of the memory consumption by generated kernels, so running all the tests as a single run may not be feasible in the future. A preferred workaround is to divide the tests to separate executables (e.g., one executable per test file).
